Throughout, we separate predictive claims (the channel integration) from generative ones (counterfactual and hedonic-asymmetry mechanisms).

articles.title: Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change
articles.authors: Douglas G. Lee; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles.abstract: Choice-induced preference change refers to the tendency for value estimates to differ after a choice relative to before it. Although this phenomenon is robust, the process that generates it remains debated. In this work, we reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies to identify empirical signatures to serve as benchmarks for candidate process accounts of choice-induced preference change. We focused on three factors that are especially informative for theory: choice difficulty, deliberation time, and the attribute structure of the options. First, we reproduced the well-established finding that the spreading of alternatives is greater for more difficult choices. Second, we showed that its relationship with response time remains after controlling for difficulty, indicating that the relationship with deliberation time is not reducible to initial value difference alone. Third, we found that preference change depends not only on overall value difference but also on how the options differ in terms of their attributes, with stronger effects for choices laden with tradeoffs than for cases of simple dominance. Together, these results indicate that choice-induced preference change is tied to deliberation itself rather than to a post hoc or artifactual revision of fixed values. The findings are compatible with both value-refinement and coherence-based reasoning accounts in some respects, but they also constrain both by showing that preference change depends jointly on difficulty, deliberation time, and attribute structure.

articles.title: Self-Efficacy Predicts Differential Neuroticism Change in a Smartphone-Based Intervention
articles.authors: Michael Dominik Krämer; Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Johannes Zimmermann; Christoph Flückiger; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Self-guided, digital interventions can help people change their personality traits in desired directions, including becoming less neurotic. However, little is known about how and why people differ in intervention-related changes. Theoretical models state that intentional personality change must be perceived as feasible and that being motivated to change is not sufficient to elicit lasting trait changes. Using a German-speaking sample (N = 446; M_age = 25.88; 85% female; Residence: 47% Switzerland, 26% Germany, 26% Austria, 1% Other), we tested whether self-efficacy and growth mindset predict change in multiple neuroticism measures across a 6-week intervention and 2-month follow-up. To isolate temporal processes during the intervention, we examined co-development of weekly neuroticism and self-efficacy and their week-to-week temporal associations. We found evidence for self-efficacy predicting differential neuroticism change but not for growth mindset. Participants with higher self-efficacy showed greater pre-post decreases in self-reported neuroticism and greater pre-post increases in emotional resilience than those with lower self-efficacy. At follow-up, participants with higher self-efficacy continued to improve more in neuroticism and emotional resilience. Last, higher self-efficacy in one week predicted lower neuroticism in the following week, and vice versa, independent of participants’ overall trajectories. In contrast, there was no consistent evidence for between-person co-development of weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism across the intervention. Findings support theoretical expectations that perceived feasibility is a precondition for neuroticism change and suggest possible reinforcement mechanisms between weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism. We discuss implications for theory and future intervention studies.

articles.title: “It’s a form of survival”: Autistic transgender and nonbinary people’s experiences of disordered eating
articles.authors: Luka White; Hazel Marzetti; Fiona Duffy; Jonah Shehata; Karri Gillespie-Smith
articles.abstract:
Autistic transgender and/or nonbinary (TNB) people are a multiply marginalised group systematically impacted by high rates of disordered eating. Feminist scholarship has examined the role of systems of oppression in creating environments where disordered eating can flourish, particularly sexism, racism and weight stigma. We expand this conversation by taking an intersectional, minority stress lens to examine the roles of cis-heteronormativity and neuronormativity in disordered eating in Autistic TNB people. Twenty-one Autistic TNB participants (aged 19-51) with disordered eating were asked to take part in narrative online interviews that were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. 
Participants framed their disordered eating as a survival technique. In line with minority stress theory, disordered eating was articulated both as a direct response to systemic and interpersonal violence, and an indirect response to internalisation of queerphobic or anti-Autistic experiences. A struggle for belonging characterised participants’ intersectional experience. Queer communities provided a site of acceptance and improved disordered eating for some, yet were also places that could exacerbate unbelonging and disordered eating through intersecting ableism, racism and fatphobia and the communication of queer-specific appearance pressures. 
Findings demonstrate the utility of an intersectional minority stress lens to examine Autistic TNB health inequities. Beyond individualised neuro- and gender-affirming approaches for Autistic TNB people with disordered eating, researchers and clinicians must move towards an emancipatory approach which considers the systemic factors influencing the mental health of this multiple minoritised community.

articles.title: Impact of an Embodied Conversational Agent on Loneliness and Emotional States in Community Dwelling Older Adults: Initial Quantitative and Qualitative Evidence
articles.authors: Feliciano Villar; Rumen Manolov
articles.abstract: The current study explores the implementation of an embodied conversational agent called AiMA at home, for community-dwelling older adults and its impact on loneliness and emotional states of older adults. Seventeen community-dwelling older adults (12 women, 5 men) líving alone participated in the study. An embodied conversational agent was implemented in their homes for 15 days. The focus of the study is placed on both qualitative and quantitative aspects. In terms of the quantitative information, the amount of interaction (days, conversations, turns) was summarized, as well as the percentage of joy and sadness. Specifically, it was found that the most frequent transition from the initial to the final emotional state across interactions, for all participants, was from neutral to joy.  In qualitative terms, participants answered an open-ended interview in which positive aspects reported of using the device and areas of improvement, were included. Results show that participants engaged and tended to engage with the ECA in an anthropomorphic way, in some cases showing a ‘human’ bond with the device. Despite both emotional and cognitive benefits were mentioned, the emotional positive impact of the interaction with the ECA (reduction of loneliness, elicitation of positive emotions) as the most frequently mentioned one. When mentioning areas of improvement, one of the aspects that participants missed was the lack of proactivity. Findings showed that participants engaged in interactions with the conversational agent, which suggests that it could a useful tool to mitigate loneliness and enhance positive emotions among older adults living alone.

articles.title: Turn-Duration Burstiness as a Temporal Signature of Collective Cognitive Demand in Multidisciplinary Healthcare Team Meetings
articles.authors: Travis J. Wiltshire; Margo Janssens; Samantha C.P. van der Bruggen; Laurens Beerepoot; Roger Leenders
articles.abstract: Collective cognition in team settings is shaped not only by what is communicated, but by the temporal dynamics of how communication unfolds. Multidisciplinary team meetings (MDTMs) in oncological care offer a naturalistic window into collective decision-making under real-world constraints, where teams of medical clinicians must jointly process complex patient cases. In this study, we examine the temporal structure of speech turn durations in oncological MDTMs using burstiness, a measure of how irregularly communication is distributed over time, as a quantitative index of communicative temporal organization. We applied two complementary burstiness metrics, the burstiness parameter (B) and the length-normalized variant (Aₙ(r)), to meeting and case-level speech turn data, and used random intercept models to examine associations between burstiness, case complexity, and case processing time. Communication was predominantly bursty, exceeding levels expected under a random process. More complex cases were associated with higher burstiness, suggesting that irregular temporal communication structure has potential to serve as an observable marker of collective cognitive load. Growth curve modeling further revealed significant main effects of burstiness and case order on case processing time, as well as interactions moderated by MDT sample. These results indicate that temporal communication dynamics and case processing is context dependent varying systematically across meeting types and as meetings progress. These findings suggest that burstiness may reflect meaningful variation in the collective cognitive dynamics of MDTMs and may offer a promising foundation for real-time monitoring of team interactions and decision-making.

articles.title: Attitudes and Affect towards Statistics in First Year Psychology Studends - a Bayesian Approach
articles.authors: Christian Seida
articles.abstract:
Statistics is regarded as one of the most difficult and frightening subjects by psychology
students. The present study develops a Bayesian framework for a more comprehensive
understanding of students´ attitudes and affect towards statistics, their development and
predictors. Furthermore, an extensive collection of related constructs was raised and analysed
psychometrically. In a longitudinal design, data of first year psychology students was collected
via online surveys at the beginning of the lectures, midst-semester and after course completion.
Four Bayesian models were fitted to inspect response patterns, pairwise item correlations and
construct change over time. In a final multilevel generalized linear varying effects model, the
effects of Statistics Anxiety on Affective Behaviours towards statistics were analysed.
Psychometric analysis yielded surprising results, as most instruments revealed insufficient
properties in the present sample. Comparative analyses revealed that Affective Behaviours
increased over the course of the semester, and Statistics Anxiety decreased. The relationship
between Affective Behaviours and Statistics Anxiety was complex, as some subscales were
correlated positively against expectations. In conclusion, the present study developed a
Bayesian framework for comprehensive data analysis, presents preliminary results of Affective
Behaviours and Statistics Anxiety and discusses a potential reliability risk in the field due to
deficient reporting of psychometric analyses.

articles.title: The Reproducible Open Coding Kit: A Human and Machine Readable Standard for Coding Qualitative Data
articles.authors: Gjalt - Jorn Peters; Szilvia Zörgő
articles.abstract: The Reproducible Open Coding Kit (the ROCK) is a standard for human- and machine-readable qualitative (coded) data. It was designed to be accessible to researchers without dedicated software, while simultaneously offering enough structure to enable programmatic processing. Through this combination and a number of features tailored to these ends, the ROCK lends itself well to facilitate application of open science principles in qualitative research, to catalyse methodological innovation in qualitative research, and to progress towards machine-readability and interoperability of (coded) qualitative data, to ultimately enable truly Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) qualitative data. In this canonical reference, we lay out the ROCK standard v1.0. We hope this allows developers to implement the ROCK in existing free and open software, stimulates the development of additional applications, and ultimately, democratizes methodological innovation in qualitative research.

articles.title: Closed-book and open-book language model assessment  of employee experience.  A two-sample convergent validity study comparing  multi-stage retrieval and single-prompt approaches
articles.authors: Richard Justenhoven; Maximilian Endress; Achim Preuß
articles.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to produce quantitative judgements about organisations from publicly available text, yet such systems differ fundamentally in whether they consult external evidence at the point of judgement or draw only on knowledge encoded during training. This study compared two systems that estimate the same 24 dimensions of employee experience using the same base language model and differ only in how evidence is gathered: a multi-stage retrieval approach, assembling each score through staged web retrieval and sequential scoring over two to three hours per organisation, and a single-prompt approach, producing all dimensions in one call from parametric knowledge. Because the two share a base model, the comparison isolates the contribution of retrieval. Evidence came from two independent samples, comprising 35 large, well-known companies and 152 organisations spanning insurance, retail, healthcare, education and professional services. Both approaches proved reliable across repeated runs (ICC(A,1) = .84 to .97). Convergence between them was moderate, with per-dimension correlations averaging .79 and .63 in the two samples and rising to .81 and .72 after correction for attenuation, and was consistently stronger for an organisation's overall score than for individual dimensions (corrected r = .91 and .85). Performance varied systematically by dimension in both samples: agreement was highest on dimensions describing an organisation's public identity, such as brand, mission and rewards, and lowest on those describing internal working experience, such as the direct manager, career progression, and diversity and inclusion. Retrieval contributed most where public text carries least, suggesting that gathering evidence determines which parts of a construct can be measured rather than simply improving accuracy.

articles.title: Why Conventional Practices in Construct Validation Provide Limited Evidence of Construct Validity
articles.authors: Leon Patrick Wendt; Steffen Müller
articles.abstract: The construct validity of psychometric instruments is a foundation of psychological science, as instruments should measure the intended theoretical constructs rather than unintended ones. Yet it has been argued that conventional construct validation practices often produce weak, uninformative evidence and fall short of the strong, risk-bearing tests emphasized by validity theorists. Extant evidence often cannot support meaningful claims about construct validity. We introduce the EVE-CV framework, based on Meehl's logic of hypothesis testing, for evaluating the evidential value (or quality) of construct validation efforts. Evidential value refers to the extent to which conducting a test of construct validity is expected to shift confidence among the proposed construct interpretation and plausible alternative interpretations. The framework translates three logical requirements for evidential value into six practical criteria for designing and evaluating construct validation studies. We also use the framework to explain how three conventional validation practices contribute to low evidential value: using conceptual placeholders, overrelying on generic psychometric methods, and revising the nomological network based entirely on evidence generated by the measure under validation. We argue that these practices are commonly used to portray instruments as “validated”, while providing only nominal evidence of construct validity.

articles.title: Revisiting Long-Term Trends in Germany’s Upper Secondary Mathematics Achievement:  A Chain Linking Analysis from FIMS 1964 to TIMSS 1996
articles.authors: Carolin Rau; Alexander Robitzsch; Aiso Heinze; Tobias Rolfes
articles.abstract:
Public discourse in many countries reflects a persistent perception of declining educational achievement over the decades, particularly among upper secondary graduates in mathematics at the transition to higher education. Assessing such claims requires evidence of long-term trends. International large-scale assessments (ILSAs), including earlier study cycles, provide a key data source, especially where systematic monitoring is lacking. In Germany, participation in ILSAs has been discontinuous and upper secondary monitoring is absent. However, data from the First International Mathematics Study (FIMS, 1964) and the Third International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS, 1996) allow the reconstruction of achievement trends over more than three decades. This study therefore estimates trends in mathematics achievement among German upper secondary graduates between 1964 and 1996 through a secondary analysis of these data.
Item response theory was used to rescale the achievement data. FIMS Germany and TIMSS Germany were chain linked via Sweden across FIMS, the Second International Mathematics Study (SIMS, 1980-82), and TIMSS using Haberman linking. Subsequently, achievement distributions for 1964 and 1996 were transformed onto the TIMSS trend scale. Sampling and linking errors were computed to assess uncertainty.
The results indicate a non-significant gain of 22 points in achievement between 1964 and 1996. Subgroup analyses reveal a significant increase in achievement for students enrolled in advanced mathematics courses, whereas no significant changes are observed for basic course levels. The decomposition of uncertainty shows that linking error substantially exceeds sampling error, indicating that trend estimates are primarily driven by item-related uncertainty. At the same time, linking error was reduced relative to a previously reported joint linking approach.
The assumption of a substantial decline in mathematics achievement over the decades cannot be confirmed. Improvements were observed among students enrolled in advanced mathematics courses. The findings suggest that chain linking can improve the precision of trend estimates when item overlap is limited and may provide a valuable approach for reconstructing trends in data-sparse contexts lacking continuous monitoring. However, linking uncertainty remains substantial, underscoring the need for additional invariant link items and systematic monitoring at the upper secondary level to support robust trend evidence.

articles.title: Dialogical Emergence in Embodied Collaboration: A Micro-Analysis of How Dyads Co-Construct Insight from Conflicting Perceptions
articles.authors: NA; Xiyuan Li; Yan Song; Xiaoyan Wang; Ze Meng
articles.abstract:
In real-time embodied collaboration, partners occupying distinct vantage points capture only local projections of the system state. When these projections conflict—for instance, when one partner perceives “pushing” while the other perceives “being pulled”—both may mistake locally valid experience for complete truth, falling into a structural illusion. Whether and how collaborators can transcend these perspectival limits through dialogue, when physical repositioning and direct perceptual sharing are infeasible, remains theoretically under-addressed.
Using partnered dance as a model system, this multi-case qualitative study recruited four established dyads who completed a standardized task and participated in dyadic synchronized video-stimulated recall interviews. Grounded in a phenomenologically-dialogical epistemology, we employed a three-tiered analytical framework—thematic content, interaction process, and identity-narrative analysis—to analyze approximately 320 minutes of recorded interview data, with segments containing perceptual divergence (totaling ~58 minutes across 16 segments) subjected to full micro-level dialogical coding.
Four major findings emerged. First, perceptual divergence reflects each partner conflating a local projection with a complete system description, signaling temporary breakdown of pre-reflective intercorporeality. Second, partners exhibited two qualitatively distinct pathways: adversarial persistence, where dialogue stagnated in repetitive cycles of negation, and integrative co-construction, where partners collaboratively discovered the partiality of their perceptions and generated emergent understanding. Third, integrative co-construction followed a recurrent six-phase micro-structure: Divergence Exposure, Pause-and-Inquiry, Individual Retrospection, Difference Localization, Emergent Reframing, and New Consensus Formation. The Pause-and-Inquiry phase—marked by clarificatory questioning—emerged as the critical juncture determining whether dialogue stalled or pivoted toward co-construction. Fourth, cognitive advancement co-evolved with partnership identification: integrative co-construction simultaneously accomplished cognitive restructuring and psychological safety restoration through shared humor and the reframing of divergence from a “relational problem” to an “information differential.”
This study articulates the micro-mechanisms of dialogical emergence, revealing a transcendence paradigm of collaborative learning—a mode in which breakthrough arises from jointly discovering perspectival limits and generating new understanding within dialogical tension. We propose collaborative epistemic restructuring as a supplement to socially shared regulation of learning and advocate shifting shared mental models research from consensus-presupposition toward difference-management.

articles.title: Italian Adaptation and Validation of the ICAR-16 Sample Test
articles.authors: Eva Tolomeo; Leognano Ceraudo; Marco Balducci; Marco Tullio Liuzza
articles.abstract: The International Cognitive Ability Resource 16 (ICAR-16) is a public-domain measure of cognitive ability. However, no Italian validation currently exists. We translated and validated the ICAR-16 in a sample of 486 Italian adults (66% females), who completed the ICAR-16 and the long version of the Cognitive Reflection Test online. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the original hierarchical structure, with the Second-Order Latent Variable model (CFI=.98; TLI=.98) showing the best fit. Moreover, the ICAR-16 correlates strongly with the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) (ϕ= .81; 95% CI: .75, .86), confirming convergent validity. Internal consistency reliability was also adequate (ωt = .82; ωh = .59; α= .78). Measurement invariance analyses supported partial scalar invariance across sexes, with no further decrement in fit indexes for strict invariance. Only one item (MR47) exhibited uniform Differential Item Functioning. Overall, these findings support the Italian ICAR-16 as a reliable, freely available instrument for cognitive assessment in research.

articles.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter: A Digital Decision Aid to Support the Selection of Communication Strategies to Overcome Language Barriers in General Practice
articles.authors: Brittany Ming Chu Chan; Julia van Weert; Hülya Ates; Jeanine Suurmond; Barbara C. Schouten
articles.abstract:
Objective: Migrant patients with limited proficiency in the host country's dominant language(s) often face difficulties in making informed decisions about selecting communication strategies to overcome language barriers. This study evaluated MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter, an evidence-based digital decision aid developed through the Spiral Technology Action Research Model with migrant patients, usability experts, and healthcare providers, using an iterative process. This approach led to MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter, designed to empower patients to select appropriate communication strategies before language-discordant medical consultations, thereby facilitating shared decision-making with their healthcare providers (HCPs) during these consultations. 
Methods: A cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) was conducted in seven Dutch general practices, involving 18 participating HCPs and 75 Turkish-Dutch patients (31 in the control group and 44 in the intervention group; Mage = 61.79, SD = 12.40), all of whom had limited proficiency in Dutch. While questionnaires assessing HCPs’ demographics and perceived communication self-efficacy were administered once before the start of the trial, questionnaires were given to patients both before and after consultations. Control patients received standard care; intervention patients used MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter prior to their consultations. 
Results: There were no differences between HCPs in the intervention and control groups regarding their perceived communication self-efficacy. On a scale from 1 to 10, they scored an average of 7.30 (SD = 1.23), indicating a high level of confidence in their ability to communicate with Turkish-Dutch patients with limited Dutch language proficiency. MediLanguage was well received for its ease of use, comprehensiveness, and attractiveness to patients. While assessments of perceived shared decision-making, perceived decisional conflict, communication self-efficacy, and patient satisfaction were conducted, only patient satisfaction showed significant improvement. 
Conclusion: Although MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter did not demonstrate clear effectiveness in improving patient-reported outcomes, it may have raised HCPs’ and patients’ awareness of the importance of addressing language barriers properly in healthcare settings. Future research should investigate how MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter can be more effectively integrated into consultations to ensure that decisions on bridging language barriers are made and implemented. This would ensure equitable access to information for all patients.

articles.title: Methodological Consistency and Measurement Standards in Mindfulness-Based Randomized Controlled Trials for Racial Minorities: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Gabriel Hall; Kyla Smith; LaTasha R Holden
articles.abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are increasingly delivered to racial minority populations, yet the methodological rigor and measurement practices underlying this literature have not been systematically evaluated. Following PRISMA guidelines, this review examined 20 U.S. randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of MBIs with samples of at least 75% racial minority participants. Each study was coded for location, adaptation type, MBI framework, control condition, solo practice, practice style, and outcome measure, and assessed for quality using modified Jadad criteria. Studies were additionally rated with the Hall et al. Mindfulness Methods Score, a novel tool developed from prior methodological recommendations. Scores ranged from 4 to 6 out of a possible 7. Reporting of intervention delivery was a consistent strength: all 20 studies described or linked their protocols, 19 described the intervention teachers, and 16 detailed the theory, content, and frequency of the practices used. Studies varied considerably in location, framework, and solo practice requirements, and none tested an un-adapted, standard MBI protocol, leaving no empirical baseline against which adaptations can be evaluated. The most consequential gap, however, concerned mindfulness itself. Eleven of the 20 studies administered no trait or state mindfulness measure, and none used a non-self-report measure. Without direct measurement of the proposed mechanism of change, neither the effect of adaptations nor the risk of adverse response can be evaluated empirically. Future research should administer explicit trait and state mindfulness measures, establish a standard-protocol baseline, and engage the methodological critiques directed at the broader mindfulness literature.

articles.title: Conditional Associations Between HEXACO Personality Traits and NEET Status in Young Adults
articles.authors: Martina Pastorelli; Anna Laura Vlad; maria esposito; Andrea Ceschi; Riccardo Sartori; Michele Scandola
articles.abstract:
Young people classified as NEET (Not in Employment, Education, or Training) represent a heterogeneous population whose educational and occupational disengagement may be shaped by the interplay between personality traits, psychological resources, and contextual conditions. Although previous research has examined several risk factors associated with NEET status, evidence on the role of personality and its interaction with self-regulatory and psychosocial resources remains limited. 

This study examined the psychological and sociodemographic correlates of NEET status in a sample of 254 young adults, including 75 NEET and 179 non-NEET participants. HEXACO personality dimensions, perceived employability, self-directed learning, future-oriented beliefs, mental health, perceived social support, education, age, and sex were assessed. Principal component analysis identified three broader dimensions: Strategic Future-Oriented Mindset, Mental Health, and Social Support. A binomial regression model showed that NEET status was associated with a complex pattern of conditional effects rather than with isolated personality traits. Strategic Future-Oriented Mindset was negatively associated with NEET status particularly at low and average levels of Honesty–Humility. Social Support was associated with a lower probability of being NEET mainly among individuals high in Extraversion. Emotionality emerged as the most stable personality-related risk factor, whereas education was negatively associated with NEET status and moderated the role of specific personality dimensions. 

These findings suggest that NEET status should be understood through a person-context framework in which personality traits interact with psychological resources and sociodemographic conditions. Interventions aimed at supporting young people at risk of educational and occupational disengagement should therefore move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches and strengthen strategic future-oriented self-regulation, interpersonal learning, emotional regulation, and the effective activation of social support.

articles.title: Exploring Public Perceptions of Social Media: A Preregistered Mixed-Methods Study
articles.authors: Evelyn Alice Halliday Murray; Michael Larkin; Daniel Shaw; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington
articles.abstract: Background: Cyberpsychology research has focused extensively on the potential impacts of social media on mental health and wellbeing. However, less is known about which platforms the public identify as “social media” and the extent to which they endorse associated positive and negative impacts. In this preregistered mixed methods study, we explored perceptions towards social media in a large sample representative of the U.K. public. Methods: Participants (n = 968, 484 adolescents) completed an online survey that asked them to identify which platforms they identified as being a “social media”, rate their level of endorsement with 68 positive and negative research-informed characteristics, and their understanding of, and agreement with, common definitions. Ninety-five participants also provided open-ended responses to questions that asked how social media had impacted themselves or others. Findings: Perceptions of which online platforms constitute “social media” varied, despite these aligning with scholarly definitions. Across age groups, participants strongly endorsed that social media is addictive, spreads misinformation, and is time-consuming, as well as being accessible and easy to use, entertaining, and updates people on local issues and news. Overall, they endorsed more negative than positive characteristics. Reflexive thematic analysis highlighted three themes of “Beyond the screen”, “Negative online behaviour” and “Removal of blame/accountability” for adults, and “Mental health concerns”, “Finding connection and support” and “Productivity concerns” for adolescents. Discussion: Understanding how the public perceives social media can inform research best practice (e.g., tailored definitions) and public policy (e.g., debates around age-restricted social media/bans).

articles.title: Uneven Effects of Decision Stakes on Advice Integration
articles.authors: Joshua Zonca; Luca Introzzi; Alice Giampino; Marco Mantovani; Paolo Cherubini; Carlo Reverberi
articles.abstract:
People often rely on human or AI advice, but whether higher stakes improve advice
integration remains unclear. Across two preregistered experiments (N = 99), participants
combined perceptual judgments with advice from artificial agents while stakes varied up to
twenty-fold. A Bayesian model provided benchmarks for optimal advice weighting. Higher
stakes prolonged deliberation but did not, on average, improve advice weighting or decision
accuracy. Instead, their effects were uneven and varied with cognitive ability. Participants
with higher ability became more optimal and accurate under high stakes, whereas those
with lower ability performed worse. Thus, incentives can mobilize effort without uniformly
improving performance and may widen differences between decision-makers. These findings
show that insufficient motivation alone cannot explain suboptimal advice integration
and identify cognitive capacity as a boundary condition on the benefits of higher stakes in
assisted decision-making.

articles.title: Vaccination as Collective Action During a Pandemic: Evidence from 6.1 Million COVID-19 Vaccination Records in Denmark
articles.authors: Lasse Hyldig Hansen; Michael Bang Petersen
articles.abstract: Classical theories in health psychology explain individuals’ decisions about whether or not to engage in protective behavior such as vaccination during a health emergency as guided by trade-offs about personal risks and benefits. Yet, vaccinations involve a clear collective action component, where individuals can protect others by getting vaccinated, beyond the personal benefits. Following recent research, we develop the argument that individual differences in the motivation to engage in collective action should influence vaccination decisions during the most significant health emergency in the 21st century, the COVID-19 pandemic, above and beyond the predictors proposed by classical theories. We test this argument by combining survey observations from 380,516 unique Danish adults with population-wide registry data on COVID-19 vaccination status for 6.1 million individuals in Denmark, of whom 4.9 million received at least one vaccine dose. Using this unique data infrastructure, we compare classical psychological correlates of protective behavior with psychological measures of individual-differences in collective action motivation. The results demonstrate collective action motivation was more strongly associated with vaccination behavior than threat appraisal or coping appraisal across the vaccination sequence, spanning completion of the recommended primary vaccination course, booster receipt, time to full vaccination, and vaccination uptake among the children of survey respondents. Furthermore, high levels of collective action motivation strongly weakened the role of personal considerations that would otherwise deter vaccination uptake, both in terms of whether or not the individual gets vaccinated and how quickly the individual gets vaccinated. These findings provide important information on the prerequisites of successful vaccination campaigns during major health crises and how governments and authorities can facilitate them.

articles.title: Top-down versus bottom-up theories of phonological acquisition: A big data approach
articles.authors: Christina Bergmann; Sho Tsuji; Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract: Recent work has made available a number of standardized meta-analyses bearing on various aspects of infant language processing.   We  utilize  data  from  two  such  meta-analyses (discrimination of vowel contrasts and word segmentation,  i.e.,  recognition of word forms extracted from running speech) to assess whether the published body of empirical evidence supports a bottom-up versus a top-down theory of early phonological development by leveling the power of results from thousands of infants.   We predicted that if infants can rely purely on auditory experience to develop their phonological categories, then vowel discrimination and word segmentation should develop in parallel,  with  the  latter  being  potentially  lagged  compared  to the  former.   However,  if  infants  crucially  rely  on  word  form information to build their phonological categories, then development at the word level must precede the acquisition of native sound categories.  Our results do not support the latter prediction.   We discuss potential implications and limitations,  most saliently that word forms are only one topdown level proposed to affect phonological development, with other proposals suggesting that top-down pressures emerge from lexical (i.e., word-meaning pairs) development. This investigation also highlights general procedures by which standardized meta-analyses may be reused to answer theoretical questions spanning across phenomena.

articles.title: Attachment and Caregiving as Social Allostatic Inference: An Updated Social Neuroscience Account from Single Brains to Dyads
articles.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Tsachi Ein-Dor
articles.abstract: Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory: individuals manage the demands placed upon their bodies not only alone but through and with others. Attachment science has pursued how the brain accomplishes this for the better part of a century, and its most recent contribution has been neurobiological. Within the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt) programme, we previously specified a neuroanatomical architecture of two interacting systems and four domain-general modules for organised attachment, extended it to attachment disruption and disorganisation, and moved it from single brains to dyads through hyperscanning as part of Relational Neuroscience. What that work established energetically, through social allostasis, it did not specify computationally. Here we close that gap. Drawing on active inference, allostasis as interoceptive inference, and recent constructs of attachment as prediction, we propose the term social allostatic inference: the attachment system is one predictive-allostatic loop, the four modules are its successive stages, and organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment are characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it. We extend the account to the caregiving system, which shares this architecture but infers rather than senses both the error that initiates its loop and the signal that terminates it. At the level of the dyad, interpersonal neural and bio-behavioural synchrony are read as indices of where regulatory work is invested rather than of bond quality directly. We address persistent misconceptions in trauma-informed practice and set out a measurement programme.

articles.title: Fear of Negative Evaluation as a Core Predictor of Eating Disorder Risk in Adolescents: A Sex-Based Analysis
articles.authors: Victoria Burmester; Dasha Nicholls
articles.abstract:
Background: Eating disorders (ED) commonly emerge during adolescence, a developmental period characterised by heightened sensitivity to social evaluation. Fear of negative evaluation (FNE), a core feature of social anxiety, may represent a key mechanism underlying vulnerability to disordered eating. This study examined FNE as a predictor of ED psychopathology in a non-clinical sample of adolescents and tested whether this relationship differs by sex.
Methods: 192 adolescents aged 16–19 completed standardised self-report measures of eating disorder symptoms (Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale-5) and FNE (Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale- revised) as part of a larger online survey. 
Results: FNE emerged as a significant and robust predictor of ED symptoms (b = 0.40, 95% CI [0.30, 0.51], p < .001), accounting for approximately a third of the variance in ED symptom scores (R² = .32–.34). Females reported significantly higher FNE and ED symptoms than males (Mann-Whitney U tests, medium effect sizes), but the relationship between FNE and ED symptoms did not significantly differ by sex (FNE × Sex interaction, b = −.13, p = .228).
Conclusions: Findings support FNE as a key predictor of ED psychopathology in adolescents. Elevated sensitivity to social judgement appears to increase vulnerability to disordered eating similarly across sexes, even though females carry a disproportionately higher burden of both FNE and ED symptoms. Targeting FNE in early intervention and prevention efforts, particularly among adolescent females, may offer a promising avenue for reducing ED risk.

articles.title: Signaling social identity in referential communication
articles.authors: Alicia M Chen; Robert Hawkins; Rebecca Saxe
articles.abstract: Any choice of words simultaneously conveys information about the world and, at the same time, conveys information about the speaker, revealing aspects of their social identity. In this paper, we investigate how speakers strategically modify referential language to signal group membership. Across four experiments using a minimal referential communication paradigm, we find that speakers with the explicit goal of signaling social affiliation (1) choose more concise utterances, (2) preferentially select group-specific referents and descriptions, and (3) resist the otherwise strong tendency to be understood by everyone in the audience. Standard models of referential communication that focus on the trade-off between informativity and efficiency cannot explain these patterns; we argue instead for a model where speakers trade off the referential utility of being understood against the social utility of being identified as an in-group member.

articles.title: Comfort in discomfort: A systematic review of pain perception in ultrarunners
articles.authors: Annabel de Jong; Allison Matthews; Mark R. Hinder; Olivia Hannon; Nathan Pitchford
articles.abstract: Pain is an inherent and expected consequence of ultrarunning (distances >42.2km). Pain perception encompasses how individuals interpret feelings of pain. Here, we systematically reviewed studies of pain management and coping, pain tolerance and threshold, experience of pain, and the impacts of pain perception on performance, within an ultrarunning context. We searched five electronic databases (MEDLINE, PsychINFO, Scopus, SportDiscus, and Web of Science), complemented with citation searches. A total 433 studies were screened, with 36 included in this review. Findings indicate that perceived pain increases during and after ultrarunning, with changes to pain intensity, sensitivity, and modulation. Pharmacological and physical interventions employed to manage pain show mixed effectiveness, with minimal impact on performance. Alternatively, maladaptive cognitive coping strategies increase the degree to which pain subjectively interferes with ultrarunning, time spent thinking about pain, and likelihood of race withdrawal, but experiential awareness reduces pain interference. Ultrarunners exhibit higher pain tolerance than non-athletes, derive moral value from pain, and actively distinguish between ‘good’ (expected) and ‘bad’ (injury-related) pain. The ability to effectively appraise manage, and tolerate pain is considered a key differentiator of high and low performing ultrarunners. Acknowledging that pain is not a unidimensional physiological phenomenon, directions for future research are discussed.

articles.title: Mental Health Supports for Caregivers of Autistic Children: An Umbrella Review
articles.authors: Tracey Chau; Yasmine Syifa Nabila Budi; Madeline Thorbecke; Alexandra Ure; Alexia Pavlis; Georgina Cox; Katrina Williams; Mohammed Alshawsh
articles.abstract:
Objective: Caregivers of Autistic children commonly report reduced mental health and wellbeing in comparison to caregivers of non-autistic children. Extensive research has demonstrated that psychological interventions improve caregiver mental health. This umbrella review aimed to (1) assess the quality and validity of systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses (SRs) that evaluated the effectiveness of clinician-delivered, non-pharmacological interventions on mental health and wellbeing outcomes in caregivers of Autistic children, and (2) synthesise evidence on the overall effectiveness of these interventions.
Method: The review was conducted in line with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for umbrella reviews. Risk of bias was assessed using the Risk of Bias in Systematic Reviews tool. 
Results: The search across seven databases identified 2227 potentially eligible records. Seventeen SRs were included, comprising n = 61 relevant primary studies and n = 1515 participating caregivers. Methodological quality of the included SRs was generally low. No SRs were considered authoritative sources for practice recommendations. Assessment of relevant studies from included SRs identified Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and psychoeducation as demonstrating the most consistent positive impact on caregivers’ self-reported symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress, as well as quality of life, and general mental health and wellbeing. Mindfulness and cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) interventions also appeared to improve symptoms in most domains to an extent, though more inconsistently.
Conclusion: Despite the poor quality of available SRs, assessment of individual studies identified ACT and psychoeducation as broad intervention modalities that strengthen caregiver psychological wellbeing. Research, practice, and policy implications are discussed.

articles.title: Parsing Exposure to Adversity: How does Caregiving Deprivation Pose a Unique Risk to Children's Adjustment?
articles.authors: Alexandria A. Baker; Patrick Davies; Vanessa T. Cao
articles.abstract: Children’s emotion perspective taking and social problem-solving are regarded as key social-cognitive mechanisms through which adverse parenting increases children’s vulnerability to social and behavioral problems. Guided by the Dimensional Model of Adversity and Psychopathology (DMAP), this study examined whether parenting threat and deprivation operate selectively or commonly through children’s emotion perspective taking and social problem-solving to increase risk to their social (i.e., peer relationship quality) and behavioral (i.e., externalizing symptomology) wellbeing. Participants included 238 children, primary caregivers, and their partners with the first of three annual measurement occasions occurring during the transition to formal school (Mean age = 4, 52% female; 68% White; 18% Black; 16% Latine, 10% multiracial, and 4% another race). Parenting deprivation and threat were assessed observationally across multiple parent-child interaction tasks. Children’s social-cognitive mechanisms were assessed using validated tasks, and teachers completed surveys of child psychological problems. Results from the fully lagged cascade model indicated that parental deprivation selectively predicted children’s subsequent social problem-solving and emotion perspective taking difficulties over and above the influence of parental threat. In the latter part of the cascade, children’s diminished emotion perspective taking predicted increases in externalizing symptoms, while children’s blunted social problem-solving predicted diminished social competence.

articles.title: Synthetic survey participants cannot substitute for sample diversity in policy
articles.authors: Sakshi Ghai; Jamie Cummins
articles.abstract: Synthetic survey participants generated by large language models (LLMs) have recently been promoted as a means of reaching diverse and underrepresented populations in policy research. We argue that this promise rests on a mistaken equivalence between demographic labelling and meaningful representation. Because LLM training corpora disproportionately reflect Western, English-language, and third-person accounts, synthetic responses may reproduce how populations are described by others rather than how their members understand and express their own experiences. We term this process etic-to-emic laundering: the transformation of external accounts into outputs that appear to be first-person testimony. Beyond methodological limitations, synthetic substitution may weaken incentives to invest in the infrastructure required for genuine inclusion, including translation, culturally grounded measurement, local expertise, community partnerships, and direct data collection. This displacement risks becoming self-reinforcing, as reduced collection of first-person data makes future synthetic samples still harder to validate. We therefore argue that synthetic participants should be confined to exploratory roles, accompanied by clear provenance disclosures, and never treated as substitutes for human respondents in policy inference. Sample diversity cannot be automated: it requires sustained engagement with the people whose lives and interests policy decisions affect.

articles.title: Self-Assessed, but Not Experimentally Induced, Rejection Sensitivity Predicts Eating Disorder Symptoms in Adolescent Girls
articles.authors: Victoria Burmester; Chloe Wong; Dasha Nicholls
articles.abstract:
Objective: Social rejection is a salient stressor during adolescence, a peak period for eating disorder (ED) onset. This study examined whether self-reported rejection sensitivity and affective responses to experimentally induced ostracism were associated with one another, and whether each independently predicted ED psychopathology, in non-clinical adolescent girls.
Method: Forty-seven girls aged 13–14 completed Cyberball and the Needs-Threat Scale (NTS), the Online and Offline Social Sensitivity Scale (O²S³), the Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale-5 (EDDS), and the Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10). Partial correlation and multiple linear regression, controlling for autistic traits, examined associations between NTS, O²S³ and EDDS scores.
Results: NTS and O²S³ scores were positively correlated after controlling for AQ-10 (r = .37, p = .009). NTS, O²S³ and AQ-10 together predicted EDDS scores (R² = .32, p < .001); O²S³ was an independent predictor (β = .43, p = .003), whereas NTS was not (β = .24, p = .104).
Discussion: Self-assessed rejection sensitivity, rather than affective responses to induced ostracism, was associated with ED psychopathology, suggesting that subjective appraisal of everyday social rejection may be more clinically relevant than acute, laboratory-induced exclusion. Rejection sensitivity may represent a useful target for early ED intervention in adolescent girls.

articles.title: Automated Classification of Restrictive and Repetitive Behaviors in Autistic Children
articles.authors: Ali Reza Omrani; Marc J Lanovaz; Davide Moroni
articles.abstract: Restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) are a common class of behavior in autistic children, and their assessment is typically based on presence and severity. While previous research has primarily focused on detecting RRBs (i.e., presence or type), automated classification of severity levels has received limited attention. The present study aimed to categorize RRB severity in 58 autistic children using clinician-labeled data based on the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS). A machine learning model was evaluated under two strategies: session-based and participant-based analyses. The model achieved high accuracy for session-based training (Cohen’s kappa = 0.82) whereas accuracy decreased for participant-based training (Cohen’s kappa = 0.54), indicating reduced generalization to new children. Confusion matrix analysis showed clearer class separation in the session-based analysis and greater overlap among ratings in the participant-based analysis. These findings suggest that the automated rating of RRBs is feasible, but that inter-individual variability remains a challenge for participant-independent applications.

articles.title: Testing predictors of change in suicide ideation among transgender and gender-diverse adults
articles.authors: Natalia Drobotenko; Caitlin Barry; Caroline Pukall; Jeremy Gordon Stewart
articles.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death worldwide and rates of suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STBs) are elevated among transgender and gender diverse (TGD) people. Longitudinal research is needed to identify predictors of STBs among TGD people and to inform gender-affirming, culturally responsive care aimed at promoting long-term well-being and reducing preventable suffering and death. The Gender Minority Stress and Resilience (GMSR) model offers a promising framework for understanding suicide-related outcomes among TGD people by emphasizing distal and proximal minority stressors alongside resilience factors – however, empirical tests remain limited. Additionally, early adversity (e.g., childhood maltreatment) and resilience are rarely integrated into tests of the GMSR model. We examined an extended GMSR model incorporating these processes in relation to suicide ideation. Participants were 382 gender-diverse adults recruited internationally who completed assessments at four timepoints over 12 months. Bivariate analyses showed that childhood maltreatment was associated with greater minority stress, lower resilience, and more frequent suicide ideation. In the longitudinal moderated mediation model, childhood maltreatment predicted greater distal minority stress, which in turn predicted elevated proximal stress four months later. However, neither distal nor proximal stress predicted subsequent suicide ideation, and resilience did not moderate these pathways. Overall, findings provide partial support for the GMSR framework in relation to minority stress processes, but do not support longitudinal pathways linking minority stress or resilience to ideation. Results highlight the importance of further examining dynamic, time-varying predictors of suicide risk in TGD populations and implications for ideation-to-action models of suicide.

articles.title: “ChatGPT Is My Best Friend”: AI as an Ambivalent Source of Social Support in Reddit Mental Health Communities
articles.authors: Rita Tang; Wenwen Cao; Yuming Fang
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) enters everyday mental health communication, people increasingly turn to chatbots for reassurance, advice, and companionship. Drawing on Social Support Theory and the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) framework, this study examined how members of ten Reddit mental health communities discuss AI in relation to mental health. We analyzed 10,042 AI-related posts, modeled their themes with structural topic modeling, measured affective language with LIWC, and estimated engagement with negative binomial models across the period surrounding ChatGPT's launch. We found thirteen themes covering every functional category of support that users sought from AI, positioning it as an informational aid, productivity assistant, therapist substitute, and companion, and also as a threat. Discussion shifted from tool-oriented uses toward clinically salient, emotionally charged themes, and its tone grew gradually more negative and anxious after the launch, diverging from a matched non-AI baseline from the same communities. Therapy-substitute and existential-threat themes drew the most engagement, whereas prevalent comfort-seeking drew little. Theoretically, the study extends social support theory by casting a nonhuman actor as a source users enlist across emotional, appraisal, informational, and instrumental functions yet also appraise as a threat, and it draws on CASA to interpret when people grant or withhold social standing to a machine. Practically, the findings inform the design and governance of AI tools already used for coping and crisis moments and highlight vulnerable users who rely on AI for private comfort yet remain least visible in peer communities. Findings position AI as an ambivalent, increasingly embedded source of support.

articles.title: Toward a Unified Perspective on Content Analysis
articles.authors: Nathan Francis Gillespie
articles.abstract: Content analysis, the practice of inferring individual difference characteristics from text data, is an important research technique across the behavioral and social sciences. The methods used to conduct it, however, are strikingly heterogenous, reflecting three distinct approaches: human-centered, dictionary-centered, and machine-learning centered. Currently, the utility of content analysis is hindered by a lack of clarity regarding how reliable, valid, and generalizable the outputs from each of these approaches are. This paper examines a cross-section of research on each approach to content analysis, evaluating each approach from the perspective of psychological measurement. Drawing on classical test theory, generalizability theory, latent variable theory, and cognitive psychometrics, I identify some potential sources of variance that shape content-analytic results. I then investigate the reliability of each approach and offer practical recommendations for future research concerning the specific situations where each approach is most appropriate. This paper suggests that the field would benefit from more theoretical cross-fertilization across camps of content analytic research practice, as well as additional work investigating the measurement processes involved in content analysis more generally. It also consolidates the essential elements of different styles of content analytic research practice and sheds light on content analysis’s strengths and limitations.

articles.title: Difficult conversations as Self-Control Conflicts
articles.authors: Yena Kim; Laura Wallace; Brad Bitterly; Emma Levine
articles.abstract: Why do people avoid having important but difficult conversations? The dominant explanation is that people are overly pessimistic about the outcomes of conversations— overestimating costs and underestimating benefits. However, anecdotal evidence suggests people still fail to initiate conversations they expect to be more beneficial than costly. We address this puzzle by testing a self-control account of difficult conversations. Like other classic self-control conflicts (e.g., going to the gym, eating healthily), we argue that engaging in difficult conversations requires people to overcome proximal, concrete costs (e.g., feeling uncomfortable, hurting someone’s feelings in the moment) in pursuit of distal, abstract benefits (e.g., helping someone grow). Across four pilot studies and six experiments (N = 2,442), we provide three key pieces of support for our account. First, people perceive difficult conversations as having intertemporal trade-offs, such that the costs precede the benefits. Second, people’s decisions to initiate difficult conversations are sensitive to time, such that people are more willing to have difficult conversations in the future than the present (i.e., they delay). Importantly, this effect is specific to conversations that are expected to have both costs and benefits, suggesting that people do not generally delay all conversations. This delay is mediated by differential weighing of the costs and benefits in addition to lower anticipated costs in the future (vs. the present). Third, people are more willing to take up costly commitment devices to motivate themselves to initiate difficult conversations than to take up equivalently costly gambles. This suggests that people are aware of these dynamics. Overall, we provide a new theoretical lens for understanding difficult conversations and point to new interventions to prompt them.

articles.title: A Review of Replication Attempts Over 88 Years of the American Speech-Language Hearing Association Journal Publications
articles.authors: Andrea Lynn Boh Ford; Jessica Salley Riccardi; Austin Thompson; Helen L Long; James C Borders; Scott R. Schroeder; Alisa Baron; Mariam El Amin; Danika L. Pfeiffer
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This review aimed to determine the prevalence of author-identified replication studies in the field of Communication Sciences and Disorders and examine longitudinal changes in this prevalence across American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) journals from 1936 to 2024. This review is a conceptual replication of Cook and colleagues’ review of replications in special education journals.
Method: Our data source comprised all 17,986 journal articles published in seven ASHA peer-reviewed journals between 1936 and 2024. We identified 3,903 articles, excluding duplicates, that contained one instance of the word replication or its stem (e.g., replicate, replicable). Two research team members independently screened articles to assess whether the study was a procedural replication aligned with our definition.  One research team member coded each article’s study metadata, CSD topic area, participants, and methods, and replication information, such as type of replication and author-reported replication success. We conducted reliability checks on 20% of articles, with an average agreement of 89.7%.
Results: Of 14,376 published studies for which a replication could have been conducted (i.e., exclusive of non-peer reviewed article types), we found 156 (1.09%) author-identified replication attempts. Most replications were conceptual (n = 122) and, according to the authors’ report, successfully replicated the previous study’s results (n = 77). The replication attempts involved a range of research designs, with experimental/quasi-experimental being the most prevalent (n = 78). Replication attempts were published more frequently over time.
Conclusions: As the first field-wide study to investigate author-identified, methodological replication attempts in CSD, our findings suggest a low rate of attempts, consistent with findings in other fields. Importantly, these replication rates represent the most conservative estimates of replication within the field, as many studies report findings that may build on previous evidence, but do not clearly identify as a direct or conceptual replication and were excluded in the current review. To continue building a cumulative and rigorous evidence base in the field of CSD, researchers should consider sharing their data and materials and completing reporting tools and checklists to clearly detail their methods and analysis processes transparently, enabling future replication. A more extensive investigation is needed to identify replication studies published in other CSD-related journals and to explore whether additional studies that use broader definitions of replication should be considered.

articles.title: Investigating the longevity of real-world memory following a smartphone intervention in older adults: A multi-year follow-up study
articles.authors: Bryan Hong; Eliza McCann; Miranda Chang; Morgan Barense
articles.abstract: Our ability to recollect details from personal past events tends to decline with age, which can affect how we act in the world, communicate with others, and understand ourselves. HippoCamera is a neuroscience-guided smartphone application that aims to mitigate these age-related memory changes by guiding users to record and review cues for real-world events using established mnemonic strategies. Previous work demonstrated improved episodic recollection and enhanced hippocampal activity for events reviewed using HippoCamera. Here, we followed up with 25 older adults 3.5 to 6 years after their participation in a HippoCamera study, using a mixed-methods approach to assess the longevity of these memory benefits. Participants reported greater subjective re-experiencing for events that were previously reviewed using HippoCamera relative to events that were only recorded but never reviewed. Further, participants reported greater subjective re-experiencing for events recorded using HippoCamera compared to events that were cued with calendar entries from a comparable time period. Using semi-structured interviews, we also explored the experience of using HippoCamera itself and reminiscing upon their past recorded events. Participants spoke to the benefits of HippoCamera not only for episodic memory, but more broadly to their daily lifestyle and activities, and their sense of meaning and well-being. Participants also reflected upon their attitudes and beliefs both towards HippoCamera and their own memory as it changes with age. Altogether, these results demonstrate the broad and long-lasting effects of a smartphone-based tool that improves memory for real-world events and enriches how older adults relate to their own past experiences.

articles.title: Reading Tiramisu in Czech and English: Robust Processing Speed Differences in Translation Equivalent Stimuli
articles.authors: Jan Chromý; Markéta Ceháková; Michael Ramscar
articles.abstract: Cross-linguistic studies of reading have documented broad similarities across languages, yet the extent to which first-language (L1) reading processes differ once structural confounds are minimized remains unclear. We conducted self-paced reading experiments in English and Czech using tightly aligned translation-equivalent sentences, enabling a direct comparison of L1 reading under parallel input conditions. Matched groups of English and Czech L1 speakers (N = 176 per language) showed near-identical comprehension accuracy but robust differences in processing speed: reaction times (RTs) were reliably faster in English than in Czech, a pattern that persisted after controlling for word length and surprisal. At the same time, the effects of classical predictors such as length and surprisal were directionally similar across languages, consistent with universal reading mechanisms. Our analyses suggest two complementary explanations for the observed cross‑linguistic differences. First, Czech exhibits higher information density than English, which—under conditions that prevent skipping and regressions—manifests as slower per‑word reading. Second, surprisal was distributed differently across the two languages: in Czech, surprisal was markedly higher at sentence onset and decreased more steeply over word position, amplifying early‑sentence processing demands. These findings indicate that while core reading processes are universal, language‑specific typological properties shape how information is packaged and distributed across the sentence, yielding systematic cross‑linguistic differences in processing speed. The results parallel cross-linguistic findings on speech rate and support an emerging framework in which reading adapts to the informational structure of the language being processed.

articles.title: The Dynamic Hierarchy of Personal Space Regulation and its Modulation by Childhood Traumatic Experiences
articles.authors: Lorenzo Lucherini Angeletti; Bianca Ventura; Giovanni Castellini; Andrew Nicholson; Ferdinando Galassi; Angelika Wolman; Josh Goheen; Sarah Masoumi; Andrea Buccellato; Benedetto Farina
articles.abstract: Personal space (PS) regulation represents a core component of socio-affective functioning, requiring the dynamic coordination of perception, affect, and behavior. Yet how these components are hierarchically organized and how adverse childhood experiences modulate this organization remain unclear. To address these gaps, 57 healthy participants underwent a computerized audiovisual stop-distance paradigm. Participants were presented with social (angry, neutral faces) and non-social (ball) stimuli approaching at two speeds. Across trials, participants stopped the stimulus at their preferred distance and rated perceived distance, perceived speed, discomfort, and threat. Bayesian multilevel modeling revealed a hierarchical Perception→Affect→Behavior architecture sustained by two functionally distinct pathways: a spatial–behavioral pathway in which perceived distance directly predicted interpersonal distance, and a temporal–affective pathway in which perceived speed predicted behavior primarily through affective elaboration. Childhood trauma was quantified using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) as a continuous measure. First, higher CTQ scores were associated with broader interpersonal distances across conditions and with amplified perceptual-affective reactivity to fast approach dynamics. Second, childhood trauma selectively restructured the spatial–behavioral pathway when stimuli were perceived as distant, shifting regulation from bodily discomfort toward anticipatory threat evaluation, while the temporal–affective pathway remained preserved. Third, higher childhood trauma scores were associated with reduced habituation of affective and behavioral responses across repeated trials. These findings characterize PS as a hierarchical dynamic regulatory system in which spatial and temporal cues engage distinct functional routes. Childhood adversity emerges as a systemic modulation that shifts the global regulatory threshold, reorganizes pathway-specific dynamics, and reduces temporal flexibility.

articles.title: Assessment of food cravings and food addiction
articles.authors: Adrian Meule
articles.abstract: This chapter briefly defines the terms food craving and food addiction and describes the most common assessment methods. These include self-report instruments such as the Food Cravings Questionnaires, the Food Craving Inventory, the Craving Experience Questionnaire, and the Yale Food Addiction Scale as well as interview measures such as the Food Addiction Symptom Inventory. It concludes by highlighting the overlaps between food craving measures and measures of food addiction as well as related constructs.

articles.title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-environmental Behaviors
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hege Landsvik
articles.abstract: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies (N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Further, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people's moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

articles.title: Beyond Universality: Do All Adolescent Minds Benefit from Mindfulness?
articles.authors: Maria Anna Wasylkowska; Pawel Holas; Dorota Kobylinska
articles.abstract: Despite the rapid global implementation of school-based mindfulness trainings (SBMTs), empirical findings regarding their effectiveness in children and adolescents remain inconsistent. Large-scale trials and recent meta-analyses have challenged early optimism, raising critical questions about for whom, under what conditions, and through which mechanisms SBMTs may be beneficial. This paper provides a synthesis of key factors, grounded in both theory and practice, that may help explain why mindfulness interventions vary in their effectiveness for adolescents. Based on existing research and insights from implementing SBMTs in school settings, we examine four interrelated domains: (1) curriculum characteristics, with particular attention to the role of embodied, mind–body practices and practice dosage; (2) the contribution of teachers, including personal mindfulness practice, embodiment, and relational engagement; (3) developmental considerations related to age, metacognitive capacity, and ethical challenges in assessment; and (4) contextual influences at the level of the school ecosystem and broader sociocultural environment. We argue that assuming universal effectiveness can overlook important sources of variability and may help explain the null or even negative outcomes reported in some studies. By reframing SBMTs as context-sensitive, developmentally attuned, and relationally embedded practices, this paper advances a conceptual framework to guide future research, intervention design, and implementation in educational settings.

articles.title: Enacting Open Science Values in Qualitative Leadership Research: Existing Practices and Future Directions
articles.authors: Camille Endacott; Brent Reed; Crystal Nicole Steltenpohl
articles.abstract: The open science movement has gained considerable momentum in advancing the transparency, credibility, and rigor of scientific research across disciplines. Within this broader landscape, leadership scholars have played a prominent role in developing formal guidance to strengthen open science practices in organizational research. To date, most recommendations have focused on quantitative research rooted in post-positivist traditions. However, qualitative scholars working from interpretivist perspectives share core values such as openness, integrity, and reproducibility with open science and enact them through practices grounded in inductive, context-sensitive inquiry. Bringing these two conversations into closer dialogue offers meaningful opportunities for both domains. Leadership research provides a particularly generative context for this exchange, as qualitative methods have influenced the field by illuminating the socially constructed and value-laden nature of leading. Drawing on these contributions, we present a set of 12 established practices through which interpretivist qualitative researchers have historically embodied open science values in leadership research, followed by six additional practices that can further enhance the openness, integrity, and reproducibility of interpretivist scholarship. By articulating how open science principles can be enacted in qualitative paradigms, we show that leadership scholars are well-positioned to extend the open science conversation across methodologies and communities of practice.

articles.title: (Computation of) the Standardized Mean Difference in Clinical Trials Should be Standardized
articles.authors: Alexander O. Crenshaw
articles.abstract: The standardized mean difference (SMD) is widely used in psychology clinical trials to convert intervention effect estimates from raw units to a common scale, enabling comparison across settings. However, multiple operationalizations of the SMD are possible for clinical trial data, with large potential impacts on estimate magnitudes. In this commentary, I review practices for operationalizing the SMD in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology and other journals that publish results of clinical trials. I find that only one-third of studies report sufficient information to determine the operationalization. Among those, the operationalization varies widely, threatening the SMD’s utility in providing a common scale. Given the common goals and design elements across many trials, it is feasible to establish a default operationalization for the SMD’s standardizer. I outline eight desirable SMD properties and evaluate each option against these properties. The pooled baseline standard deviation meets seven of eight, far more than any alternative, with its main limitation being susceptibility to inflation from restrictive inclusion criteria. I conclude that raw effect estimates should be divided by the pooled baseline standard deviation as a default, one-size-fits-most choice. Adopting this standard will help the SMD meet its promise as a standardized metric, improving comparability of results across different measures, outcomes, studies, and populations. I also provide reporting recommendations to improve transparency and enable re-computation using alternative standardizers when needed.

articles.title: Understanding the morality of unbelievers: Secular beliefs about right and wrong in ten countries
articles.authors: Roosa Haimila; Tiina A M Parkkinen; Eva Kundtová Klocová; Everton de Oliveira Maraldi; Hugh Turpin; Miguel Farias; Valerie van Mulukom
articles.abstract: Many people around the world believe that to be moral, one must believe in God. However, individuals who do not believe in God also hold distinct ethical beliefs. Similar to theists, non-theists in different cultures may share overarching narratives about morality and what it is founded upon—a possibility that remains understudied. In the present research, we utilised open-ended survey data to explore what non-theists from ten countries (N = 996) described as the basis of their views on right and wrong. We also investigated how different beliefs about morality clustered together. The findings show diversity but also point towards cross-culturally recurring patterns in non-theistic beliefs and belief clusters concerning 1) important moral principles and 2) perceived sources of morality. We furthermore discuss country-specific findings, such as the importance of ‘conscience’ for Turkish and Czech participants and ‘cultural Christianity’ in the Danish sample. Altogether, the results support research indicating that a lack of belief in God does not entail moral relativism and question views on non-theists primarily seeing morality as self-constructed. Instead, our findings point towards a more prominent role of social interaction and ‘social contract’ in views about the basis of right and wrong. In light of the results, we suggest that predominant ways of measurement in moral psychology may currently obscure diversity in non-theistic moral outlooks, such as more communal secular ethics. The main limitation of the research is convenience sampling. We therefore encourage future work to utilise representative samples to explore differing secular moralities and their predictors.

articles.title: Interpreting FMS and SSQ Cybersickness Ratings via User Tolerance in Virtual Reality
articles.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Michael Dorneich; Stephen Gilbert
articles.abstract: Cybersickness remains a persistent challenge limiting the usability of virtual reality (VR), yet commonly used subjective measures such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) and the Fast Motion Sickness (FMS) scale are often difficult to interpret in terms of user outcomes.
