In particular, there is limited guidance on how specific values on these scales relate to user tolerance or the likelihood that users will discontinue a VR experience due to discomfort. This work addresses this gap by calibrating cybersickness severity interpretations against early termination of a VR experience. In Study 1 (N = 183), participants played an immersive VR game for up to 20 minutes and were free to terminate the experience at any time. Using a Behavioral Risk Banding (BRB) framework, logistic regression linked a modified 0-10 version of the FMS (FMS-10) and post-exposure SSQ scores to dropout probability, yielding behaviorally grounded risk severity bands (mild, moderate, severe, extreme). Survival analyses then showed how these bands mapped onto tolerance over time, revealing a transitional region marked by heightened individual variability. Study 2 (N = 304) evaluated the robustness of these categories across variation in VR content and mitigation context by applying the Study 1 thresholds without re-estimation. Although absolute dropout risk varied, the ordering and behavioral meaning of severity categories were preserved. Together, these results provide a practical, behaviorally grounded framework for interpreting cybersickness ratings in terms of user tolerance and usability across VR contexts.

articles.title: Creativity Geometry: Recursive Creative Self-Improvement Through System-3 Metacognitive Scaffolding
articles.authors: Juan Carlos Chávez-Autor
articles.abstract: Human creative cognition and frontier artificial intelligence increasingly confront the same higher-order problem: how to generate possibilities, evaluate them, integrate feedback, preserve meaningful diversity, and use previous experience to improve future creative activity. Existing accounts often isolate one part of this process. Creativity research commonly emphasizes novel and useful products; dual-process theories emphasize associative and analytic modes; artificial-intelligence research emphasizes generation, self-correction, agents, tools, or self-modification. None of these alone explains when recurrence becomes recursive creative self-improvement. This Conceptual Analysis introduces Creativity Geometry, a meta-theoretical framework centered on Generation, Reflection, Integration/Iteration, and Metacontrol (GRIM) across Time. These are not proposed as independent modules or a literal mathematical law, but as interdependent functions defining the relational shape of creative transformation. System-3 denotes the metacognitively governed configuration that regulates when to broaden search, constrain it, reorganize representations, seek feedback, continue, or commit. Novelty, usefulness, and diversity (NUD) independently evaluate the resulting creative repertoire; diversity is treated as a set- and population-level condition that protects future option value. In biological cognition, the framework is grounded in creative metacognition, embodied valuation, default-executive network cooperation, confidence and error monitoring, and neuromodulatory regulation of effort, persistence, exploration, and switching. In artificial systems, System-3 is a functional analogue involving generators, critics, memory, integration, telemetry, and bounded control, without implying consciousness or organismic purpose. Evidence from large-language-model self-correction, code refinement, automated scientific discovery, creativity benchmarks, and human-AI collaboration reveals both the promise of recursive workflows and the risks of evaluator dependence, homogenization, and recursive collapse. Creativity Geometry defines recursive self-improvement as improvement in the scaffold governing future creative cycles, demonstrated through independent evaluation, transfer, stability, traceability, and preserved diversity. The result is a conceptual foundation for the science of human creativity and the responsible development of recursively improving AI.

articles.title: The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ):  Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening
articles.authors: Dominique T Vuvan; Julia Cannistraro; Rachel Goodkind; Megha Sharda
articles.abstract: Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener’s cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics versus the other musical features (i.e., pitch, rhythm, timbre). In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to reduce 121 candidate items down to 12 items for the LFQ. In Study 2, we used confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency measures to ascertain the unidimensional structure of the LFQ. In Studies 3 and 4, we demonstrated that the LFQ is correlated to comprehension of lyrics but not to the ability to exactly recall lyrics. In Study 5, we aggregated data from the first four studies to create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and to explore discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. The LFQ is presented as a practical, valid, and reliable tool for researchers interested in the relation between music and language.

articles.title: Self-Construal, Sense of Belonging, Perceived Match, and Persistence Intentions: Exploring Intersecting Identities and Moderation Effects
articles.authors: Ordene Edwards; Maci DeMott
articles.abstract: Prior research has examined the relationships among self-construal, sense of belonging, perceived match, persistence intentions, and demographic factors. However, investigations often overlook the intersecting identities of race, gender, and generation status. Furthermore, little is known about how these demographic factors moderate the relationship between these psychosocial factors and persistence intentions. This study explored self-construal, perceived match, sense of belonging, and persistence intentions at the intersection of race, gender, and generation status. We also examined how these characteristics influence the relationship between these psychosocial factors and persistence intentions. Participants were introductory psychology students (N = 1,496). Three-way ANOVAs revealed one significant three-way interaction for interdependent self-construal, favoring Hispanic continuing-generation (CG) female students over Hispanic CG males, albeit with a small effect size. Additionally, moderation analysis revealed that independent self-construal more strongly influenced persistence intentions among first-generation students than CG students. Theoretical and practical implications of the findings are discussed.

articles.title: Relative weighting of visual and auditory cues in street-crossing decisions with age-related macular degeneration
articles.authors: Daniel Oberfeld; Patricia R. DeLucia; joseph kearney; Melissa Cloutier; Anna M. Jilla; Audrey Taylor; Charles C. Wykoff; Robin Baurès
articles.abstract: We investigated street-crossing decisions in individuals with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) compared to a group with normal vision, using highly realistic visual and acoustic simulations of a vehicle approaching a pedestrian. Participants pressed a button at the last safe moment they could safely start crossing the street. The vehicle was presented visually, auditorily, or both concurrently. We present a novel analysis method for estimating the relative importance of visual and auditory cues for the crossing decision. In single-modality conditions, cue weights indicated that responses were associated not only with the vehicle's arrival time (i.e., gap duration), as it would be if decisions were based on an unbiased estimate of the arrival time, but also with the vehicle’s spatial distance, optical size, acoustic vehicle source intensity, and with time elapsed after the trial start. In the audiovisual condition, auditory and visual cues were associated with the responses. Results are largely compatible with cue weights in arrival time estimates made by the same participants, reported in a previous paper. The cue weights showed minor differences between the groups with AMD and normal vision. Analyses of the mean judged shortest safe gaps and their intraindividual variability showed effects of vehicle speed, source intensity, and size, compatible with the cue weights and TTC estimation results from our previous paper, but again with minor differences between the two groups. However, the proportion of safe crossing decisions was lower in the AMD group, due to a slower walking speed. Our study provides important insights into the decision-making in crossing decisions and shows that AMD had a surprisingly small effect on such decisions.

articles.title: Meditation Fosters Bonding and Cooperation with Humanity and All Forms of Life
articles.authors: Liudmila Gamaiunova; Harvey Whitehouse
articles.abstract: Altruism in social species, including humans, typically favors genetically close individuals. But humans also show altruism toward non-related individuals who share religious beliefs, ethnic origins, or national identities. This study explores whether Buddhist contemplative training fosters identity fusion—a strong, kin-like psychological bond—with humanity at large and all forms of life on Earth. In a cross-sectional design, 418 Buddhist meditation practitioners and 418 age and gender-matched non-practitioners completed measures of identity fusion and related mechanisms, such as perceived shared biology and empathy-related affective states. Participants also performed a semi-hypothetical donation task. Results showed that practitioners reported significantly higher identity fusion with both humans and animals and made larger donations to humanitarian and animal-protection charities. Meditation impacted underlying mechanisms differently: perceived shared biology increased more for animals, while empathy-related states increased more for humans. Both mechanisms mediated the link between contemplative practice and identity fusion. In turn, identity fusion partially mediated the relationship between meditation and charitable giving, suggesting that fusion with the target group influenced altruistic behavior. These findings suggest that contemplative training may help to extend the cooperative benefits of identity fusion with unrelated individuals, and even with other species.

articles.title: Cognitive functions in childhood apraxia of speech: A scoping review
articles.authors: Shina Jinn Cook; Edwin Maas
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Children with childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) often have co-occurring difficulties in language, learning, motor, and sensory function, but the neurological bases of the disorder are debated. A domain-general theory suggests that CAS may involve cognitive domains beyond motor-speech function. The purpose of this scoping review is to evaluate the state of the evidence describing cognitive functions in CAS and identify gaps to guide future research in elucidating the nature of the disorder.  

Method: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines were used. Five databases were searched to identify articles, supplemented with citation chasing. Included articles were charted by purpose, design, and CAS diagnostic confidence.  

Result: Seventeen articles published between 1979 and 2022 met inclusion criteria following full-text review. Studies primarily examined sequential processing, procedural learning, working memory, and executive function. Most studies used comparative designs. Across studies, participants with CAS demonstrated difficulties on cognitive tasks compared to controls or normative data. Variability in participants, measures, methodology, and diagnostic confidence limits the generalizability of findings.  

Discussion: Despite methodological variability, findings broadly support the investigation of domain-general cognitive mechanisms in CAS. Further research using replication, longitudinal designs, and ecologically valid assessments is needed to delineate the relationship between CAS and cognitive functioning.

articles.title: High-frequency visual stimulation can increase medial temporal lobe ripple oscillation density
articles.authors: Julian Keil; Victor Hernandez-Urbina; Liam Doherty; Hamed Bahmani; Martin Holtkamp; David Steinbart; Alexandra-Dikorey Diall; Jonas Hebel; Christian Brandt; Thomas Cloppenborg
articles.abstract:
Background: Flickering visual stimulation can evoke neural oscillations, which can influence ongoing brain activity. Electrophysiological recordings of neural oscillations in the ripple band (80-180 Hz) showed that these high-frequency oscillations occur in the neocortex and the hippocampus, that they phase-synchronize across long distances, and that ripple oscillations in the neocortex often precede those in the hippocampus during wakefulness. It is therefore possible that the neocortical ripple oscillations propagate beyond sensory areas to the hippocampus, inducing ripple oscillations. 
Methods: To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment (N = 8) in humans, using ultra-high frequency visual stimulation (UHV-stimulation) to evoke ripple oscillations recorded through electrodes implanted in or near the hippocampus. Although hippocampal ripple oscillations, so-called sharp-wave-ripples (SWRs), mostly occur during quiet rest or slow-wave-sleep, we aimed to increase their abundance using visual stimulation during wakefulness. We hypothesized that UHV-stimulation would increase the number of SWRs relative to an eyes-open resting-state baseline. 
Results: In line with this hypothesis, we observed significantly more SWRs per second during periods of stimulation compared to a resting-state baseline before and after the stimulation. 
Conclusion: This indicates that UHV-stimulation can be used as a safe noninvasive tool to influence SWRs, which offers the potential to improve memory.

articles.title: “How Do You Feel?” Direct Valence Measurement Enables the Detection of Affect Shift Dynamics as Powerful Predictors of Psychological Well-Being
articles.authors: Carmen Goicoechea; Pandelis Perakakis
articles.abstract: Valence is central to affective experience yet remains poorly operationalized in emotion science. Most research infers valence by categorizing discrete emotions as positive or negative, which may conflate distinct aspects of emotional experience. On the other hand, direct bipolar valence measurement—asking individuals "How do you feel?" on a continuum from negative to positive—allows participants to integrate contextual complexity into their affective reports. Critically, this approach also enables the detection and quantification of transitions between positive and negative affective states, opening new possibilities for studying affect dynamics. We tested whether metrics quantifying these directional transitions predict psychological well-being more effectively than traditional intensity-based measures. Across three ecological momentary assessment datasets with 345 participants and over 30,000 assessments, the positive to negative affect shift ratio—quantifying the propensity to transition from positive to negative affect—showed stronger predictive associations with well-being outcomes than means and standard deviations derived from the same valence scale. This pattern persisted across LASSO regression, hierarchical regression, and relative importance analyses, and remained robust even with only 3 daily assessments. These findings demonstrate that direct valence measurement offers both theoretical advantages by respecting participant-integrated experience and empirical advantages by enabling more predictive dynamics metrics, while remaining practical for clinical applications.

articles.title: Testing the impact of filtering harmful posts: A randomized-controlled trial with 100.000 users on Nextdoor
articles.authors: David Joachim Grüning; Matthew Katsaros
articles.abstract: We investigate the effectiveness of an intervention designed to filter offensive content on the local social media platform Nextdoor. The intervention, commonly used across large social platforms, was tested through a randomized controlled trial involving 100,000 people over nine months. We evaluated whether filtering content impacted fifteen different measures of platform behavior including views of offensive posts, visits to the platform, content consumption, and content production. This randomized-controlled experiment was an advanced followup-study of a Nextdoor-study (Katsaros et al., 2023) conducted a year before, showing mostly null effects of the intervention. In this study, the results showed a significant reduction in two target outcomes - views of offensive posts and comments - in the treatment group compared to the control group. However, as in the past Nextdoor-experiment, we observed no significant effects of the intervention on the thirteen measured outcomes between groups. This study provides empirical evidence on the impact of a prominent and commonly used intervention and highlights its limitation, demonstrating the complexity of effectively moderating online platforms.

articles.title: Interpersonal Extrinsic Dysregulation: Rethinking Emotion Dysregulation Across Childhood
articles.authors: Evelyn Mary-Ann Antony; Sarah A Walker; Nadin Beckmann
articles.abstract:
Interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation refers to persistent yet miscalibrated or dysregulating attempts to influence others’ emotional states, and 2) pervasive avoidance of emotionally charged interpersonal situations. We conceptualise interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation as distinct from intrapersonal emotion dysregulation and related interpersonal phenomena (e.g., co-rumination, empathy, and parentification), as it specifically concerns the child's role as a regulator of others’ emotions and the systematic miscalibration or avoidance of this regulatory function. This paper presents an integrative developmental framework that conceptualises interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation as a reciprocal process embedded within emotional exchanges across family, peer, and educational contexts. Drawing on attachment theory, social-cognitive learning theory, and reinforcement learning perspectives, we propose that maladaptive interpersonal regulatory orientations emerge through the cumulative effects of early relational experiences, observational learning, and contingently reinforced emotional behaviours. We further examine how stressors across multiple domains, including family conflict, academic pressures, and broader socio-cultural inequalities, may interact over time to exacerbate dysregulation and undermine psychosocial functioning. Extending this across childhood, we outline how interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation may manifest differently from early to late childhood as regulatory capacities and interpersonal demands evolve. We conclude by identifying key priorities for future research, including the need for longitudinal, multi-informant, and observational approaches to clarify the developmental origins, differentiation, and consequences of interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation. By providing the first integrative framework for this construct, this paper aims to advance understanding of children's interpersonal emotion regulation and its role in socioemotional development.


Keywords: emotion dysregulation, interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation, emotion development

articles.title: Measuring Reputation and Identity Effects in Multiple Rater Assessments: Guidelines for Specifying Trait Reputation Identity Models
articles.authors: Lukas Aaron Knitter; Michael Eid; Tobias Koch
articles.abstract: Multirater assessments are widely used in psychology to seperate what targets report about themselves from what others perceive about them. The Trait–Reputation–Identity (TRI) model provides a prominent modeling approach for this purpose, but applications of the model often yield improper solutions, including negative variances and weak or inadmissible factor loadings. We argue that these problems arise because the original TRI model does not sufficiently distinguish between different rater types and designs. Building on stochastic measurement theory, we show that TRI model components have different meanings depending on whether observers are interchangeable or structurally different raters. For interchangeable observers, the common observer perspective is already represented by an observer-trait factor. Consequently, the reputation effect cannot be modeled as a higher-order factor. Moreover, identity and reputation effects must be estimated in separate models. For structurally different observers, different TRI models can be specified to answer different substantive questions. We derive different design-oriented TRI models, define variance components for trait, reputation, identity, and rater-specific effects, and illustrate the approach with empirical examples. The proposed framework clarifies the interpretation of TRI effects and provides practical guidelines for specifying TRI models.

articles.title: National Predictors of Conspiracy Beliefs: A Machine Learning Analysis of Cross-Country Data
articles.authors: Sinan Alper; Caspar J. Van Lissa; Karen Douglas; Robbie M. Sutton
articles.abstract: Conspiracy beliefs vary widely across nations, yet their societal predictors remain poorly understood. Applying machine-learning meta-analytic techniques, we simultaneously examined 18 national-level developmental and cultural factors and ranked their relative importance in predicting conspiracy beliefs. Across six large cross-national datasets (total N = 178,789; 72 countries), the best-performing model (MetaForest) explained 43% of variance in test data. Corruption was the strongest predictor, followed by power distance, reading proficiency, individualism, mathematics proficiency, human development, GDP, and science proficiency. Conspiracy beliefs were most prevalent in societies marked by higher corruption and power distance, and lower educational performance, individualism, and socioeconomic development; developmental indicators generally outranked cultural ones, and dimensions such as WEIRDness, uncertainty avoidance, and long-term orientation mattered little. By integrating developmental and cultural predictors in a single framework, this study offers the most comprehensive test to date of national correlates of conspiracy beliefs and demonstrates the value of machine-learning approaches.

articles.title: La reconnaissance des mots dans la parole accentuée : Une étude en laboratoire et à l’extérieur.
articles.authors: Delphine Deï; Page Elizabeth Piccinini; Isabelle Dautriche; Marieke van Heugten; Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract: Mispronunciations slow down word recognition: A study using touchscreens in the lab and the real world. Recent work suggests that children and adults are initially delayed when exposed to an accented talker, but quickly recover and develop talker-specific listening patterns. This research, however, is often carried out in the lab, where participants’ attention is focused on a single task and no distractions are present, and recovery is often deduced from looking patterns that require little overt response. In this experiment, we overcome these limitations and assess children’s and adults’ word recognition in accented speech, tested in both a laboratory and in a naturalistic setting. We found that mispronunciations in accented speech slow down overt decisions about word recognition, to a similar extent in the lab and in familiar environments, for both children and adults.

articles.title: Facial expression synchrony is associated with neural synchrony during mother-infant interactions
articles.authors: Debora Suppiger; Tilman Reinelt; Sabino Guglielmini; Martin Wolf; Judith M. Burkart; Nathalie Giroud; Moritz M. Daum; Giancarlo Natalucci; Paola Cerrito
articles.abstract: Social interactions depend on the temporal coordination of multiple behavioral and neural processes. This coordination, known as interpersonal synchrony, is thought to support communication and shared understanding, yet how different synchrony modalities relate to one another remains unclear. Here we examined facial expression and neural synchrony during naturalistic play in 86 mother–infant dyads (infant age 7.4 months). Facial expression synchrony was quantified using automated facial action unit coding and windowed cross-lagged correlations, while neural synchrony was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and wavelet-transform coherence across prefrontal and temporo-parietal regions. Mothers and infants showed strong facial expression synchrony, during approximately 40 % of the interaction and consistent neural synchrony across cortical regions. The two synchrony modalities were related, but associations were localized and bidirectional, suggesting that synchrony across modalities does not arise from a single underlying process. Instead, synchrony may emerge from multiple interacting systems that support flexible social exchange.

articles.title: Cognitive Function and Return to Work: Protocol for a Longitudinal Study Investigating Cognitive Endurance in Stress-Related Disorders
articles.authors: Hanna Malmberg Gavelin; Anastasiya Zakrevska; Magnus Johansson; Anna Nordberg; Elisabeth Björk Brämberg; Fabienne I.M. van Vliet; Birgit H.P.M. Donker-Cools; Frederieke Schaafsma; Anna Finnes
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Patients with long-term stress-related disorders report cognitive symptoms across a broad range of domains; however, neuropsychological test results often do not align with these self-reported cognitive difficulties. One potential explanation for this discrepancy is that patients may perform well during a single, undisturbed test session but have difficulties sustaining cognitive performance over time following prolonged mental effort, which can be conceptualized as reduced cognitive endurance. This may have implications for work participation and hinder return to work unless adequately addressed. 

Methods and analysis: This study protocol describes a longitudinal study aimed at investigating cognitive endurance in patients with long-term stress-related disorders. Moreover, we will explore the association between cognitive endurance and each of the following variables: self-reported fatigue and cognitive function, self-assessed work ability, and return to work. Sixty patients with long-term stress-related disorders will be recruited from a nonrandomized multicentre controlled trial evaluating work-focused cognitive behavioural therapy in a primary healthcare setting. Sixty healthy controls will be recruited through advertisement. Cognitive endurance is assessed through repeated cognitive testing in the morning and afternoon of a regular working day, at two time points: baseline and six months after study enrolment. The cognitive tests focus on short-term and working memory, attention and processing speed, and executive functions. Prior to the assessments, participants complete questionnaires concerning trait fatigue, self-reported cognitive function and work ability. Moreover, state fatigue is assessed through self-report questionnaires administered during the assessment day. Sick-leave registry data is used to investigate return to work for the patient group. The study evaluates a novel method for assessing cognitive functioning in stress-related disorders and can provide insights into how variations in cognitive functioning over the course of a workday relate to different aspects of fatigue, as well as to functioning in everyday life and at work.

Ethics and dissemination: The study has been approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Dnr 2025-01713-01; 2025-07089-02). All participants will receive written and oral information about the study and provide written informed consent. Results will be disseminated in peer-reviewed scientific journals, at academic conferences and through communication with key stakeholders. 

Trial registration: The trial was registered 2 April 2026 at the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CYSGX).

articles.title: Learning Goals and Listening in Polarized Conversations: A Test Across Four Labs
articles.authors: Kenneth G DeMarree; Guy Itzchakov; See Ya Hui Michelle; Netta Weinstein; Taylor Lee; Yaara Turjeman-Levi; Angelia Venezia
articles.abstract: Disagreements often feel threatening, leading people to respond defensively, which can intensify both attitude and social polarization. High-quality listening is a key strategy thought to reduce polarization in these interactions, but this type of listening is rarely employed when disagreeing partners converse, and little is known about how to encourage it. To address this gap, we tested whether conversational goals, specifically, adopting goals to learn about one’s conversational partner versus a goal to persuade one’s conversational partner, can improve high quality listening and, in turn, reduce attitude and social polarization during disagreements. We hypothesized that learning goals foster perceptions of high-quality listening behaviors, which in turn increase partners’ psychological safety, promote open-mindedness, and ultimately reduce polarization. We conducted a large, preregistered experiment across four sites (Israel, Singapore, the U.K., and the U.S.; Total N = 1407). Using live dyadic conversations between strangers who disagreed on a focal topic, we manipulated one participant’s conversational goal and assessed both partners’ experiences. The goal manipulation did not influence perceived listening quality or polarization outcomes in any sample. However, preregistered path analyses provided consistent support across the four labs for the listening-to-depolarization portion of the hypothesized model: Perceived listening quality positively predicted increased psychological safety, which in turn predicted increased open-mindedness and many of the assessed indicators of polarization. The findings highlighted both the need for, and the difficulty of, encouraging high-quality listening during disagreements, with implications for understanding and improving polarization.

articles.title: Word-Level Measures of Syntactic Complexity in Sentence Processing: An Organizing Review
articles.authors: Cas W. Coopmans; Noa Talker-Aharoni; Galit Agmon
articles.abstract: The recent adoption of naturalistic paradigms in the psychology and neuroscience of language has necessitated methods for quantifying incremental syntactic processing complexity. However, there is little consensus about how complexity should be quantified. Existing studies employ a wide range of complexity metrics, reflecting divergent assumptions about the nature of grammatical representations and the mechanisms underlying syntactic processing. Because these assumptions are rarely made explicit, findings across studies cannot be reliably interpreted or consistently synthesized into general conclusions. The goal of the present study is to review the word-level syntactic complexity metrics that have been used to model behavioral and neural measures of syntactic processing. To organize the empirical literature, we introduce a taxonomy based on two complementary dimensions: the grammatical distinction between constituency and dependency representations, and the cognitive distinction between computation- and memory-related aspects of syntactic processing. Our review reveals substantial heterogeneity in how syntactic complexity is operationalized and interpreted, even among ostensibly similar metrics. To test this quantitatively, we applied hierarchical clustering to 26 metrics computed on a sample of 100 annotated sentences. Computation- and memory-related metrics largely clustered together, providing quantitative support for the relevance of our proposed taxonomy. However, this pattern emerged only when constituency- and dependency-based metrics were analyzed separately, showing that the choice of the grammatical formalism shapes how syntactic complexity is quantified. Taken together, these findings underscore the need for greater conceptual clarity in the use of syntactic complexity metrics and for more explicit linking hypotheses connecting linguistic structure to cognitive and neural processes. This review provides a useful framework for achieving these goals.

articles.title: Beyond Behaviour: Autistic Students' Self-Reported Experiences and Expression of Well-Being at School
articles.authors: Annette Carroll; Kate Simpson; Kathryn Ambrose; Dawn Adams
articles.abstract: Autistic students are increasingly represented in mainstream classrooms, yet for many, school remains a source of stress and misunderstanding. While existing research has largely focused on adverse outcomes for autistic students, less attention has been given to identifying indicators of well-being and understanding how it is experienced in everyday school settings. This study addresses this gap by centring autistic students’ perspectives through a flexible, multi‑modal qualitative design. Twelve autistic primary and secondary students shared their experiences through interviews, drawings, written responses, and photovoice methods tailored to their communication preferences and strengths. Data were analysed using inductive content and reflexive thematic analysis. Students described diverse indicators of well‑being across emotional, social, sensory‑physical, and academic domains. High well‑being was often reflected in engagement in learning, access to effective self‑regulation strategies, and expressions of joy, while low well‑being often led to withdrawal, reduced communication, tense posture, and expressions of sadness. Thematic analysis of student experiences highlighted how autistic student well‑being is frequently misunderstood or overlooked. Overall, autistic student well‑being emerged as relational, context‑dependent, and individually patterned, drawing attention to the ways it may be variably expressed, recognised, and responded to in school settings.

articles.title: 90% mental, 10% physical? Psychological and physiological predictors of ultrarunning performance
articles.authors: Annabel de Jong; Allison Matthews; Mark R. Hinder; Nathan Pitchford
articles.abstract: Within the ultrarunning community, performance is often considered ‘90% mental, 10% physical’. This demonstrates the influence of both psychological and physiological factors, particularly emphasising the perceived dominance of psychology. However, extant research typically considers psychological or physiological variables in isolation. Additionally, studies frequently recruit participants from a single ultramarathon, thereby neglecting heterogeneity between events. The current study addresses these limitations by employing an interdisciplinary approach and recruiting participants from a range of races to develop a robust, predictive model of ultrarunning performance. Ultramarathon participants (n = 69 across 24 events) underwent graded exercise testing, psychometric surveys, and physiological/cognitive assessments (Cold Pressor, Stop-Signal, and Serial Sevens tasks). Performance was quantified as percentile finishing time relative to gender-matched event winners. Selection of the initial 15 candidate variables was informed by evidence from relevant literature. A single global model was developed using backwards stepwise regression (Aikake Information Criterion selection), including four covariates: age, gender, apparatus, and distance. The overall model (p < .001, adj. r2 = .426) included VO2max (ß = .609), emotional intelligence (ß = .281), inhibitory control (ß = .259), and sleep behaviours (ß = .226) as key significant predictors. These results demonstrate that the predictability of ultrarunning performance is improved by moving beyond traditional metrics of fitness and considering both psychological and physiological variables. Overall, this model provides an integrated approach for maximising endurance sports training and performance, with broader application to other fields involving physical and psychological exertion (e.g., military, pain management).

articles.title: When Does Prayer Promote Flourishing? Attachment, Prayer Profiles, and Psychological Flourishing
articles.authors: Aaron D. Cherniak; Pehr Granqvist; Mario Mikulincer
articles.abstract: Prayer is among the most prevalent human behaviors, yet its psychological benefits are inconsistently documented. Most research relies on unidimensional measures and overlooks the relational dynamics that shape the function of prayer. The present study examined associations between attachment to God, latent prayer profiles, and flourishing in a sample of N = 452 Israeli Jews (M age = 44.69, SD = 14.96; 48.0% female). Participants completed the Multidimensional Prayer Inventory (MPI), the Attachment to God Inventory (AGI), and the Harvard Flourishing Measure. Latent profile analysis of MPI subscales identified four prayer profiles: Modal, Disengaged-Habitual, Engaged-Devotional, and Engaged-Penitential. Profiles differed significantly in flourishing and AGI scores: the Disengaged-Habitual profile showed the highest AGI avoidance and the lowest flourishing, whereas the Engaged-Devotional profile showed the lowest AGI anxiety and the highest flourishing. Hierarchical regression revealed that only the Disengaged-Habitual profile predicted significantly lower flourishing relative to Modal prayer, while AGI anxiety and avoidance were the dominant predictors. Interaction analyses showed that  AGI anxiety was less strongly associated with lower flourishing for the Engaged-Penitential profile. These findings underscore the centrality of relational orientation toward God in shaping the psychological function of prayer and inform a person-centered understanding of when and for whom prayer promotes flourishing.

articles.title: What’s Brown and Sticky? Peering Into the Ineluctable Comedic Mystery of Dad Humor with a Handful of Machine Learning Models, Hundreds of Humans, and Tens of Thousands of Dad Jokes
articles.authors: Paul Joseph Silvia; Meriel I. Burnett
articles.abstract: A stick, of course. This masterpiece of human creativity is an example of a dad joke, a clean, good-natured joke founded on puns, literalism, and wordplay. After unpacking the structures, contents, and comedic devices that distinguish dad jokes from related genres, the present research explored both the features of dad jokes that make them funny and the kinds of people who find them funny. Study 1 coded over 32,000 jokes scraped from the Reddit r/dadjokes community. Ridge regression models found that a joke’s upvotes and comments were modestly predictable from its text and topic features (test sample R2 = 4.02% and 4.42%). After curating a hypercube subsample of 501 dad jokes, Study 2 found that both text features (e.g., concreteness, semantic distance, question framing) and topic features (e.g., moms, pregnancy, and numbers) predicted the funniness ratings made by adults (n = 621) much more effectively (cross-validated R2 = 28.2%). Study 3 found that individual differences in people’s funniness ratings were associated with cultural conventionality (e.g., parenthood, more education, affluence, religiosity, and conservatism) and social boldness (e.g., need for uniqueness, low honesty-humility, and boldness; cross-validated R2 = 32.4%), and that dads found the dad jokes funnier. Seemingly simple wordplay humor illuminates the psychology of verbal creativity and extends the psychology of aesthetics into art encounters that provoke feelings of amusement, playfulness, and absurdity. The coded dad jokes are freely available for researchers interested in studying humor or hassling their teenagers.

articles.title: From Seeing to Describing: A Pictogram-based method for investigation the vision-language interface
articles.authors: Brenda Corchado-Robles
articles.abstract:
Visual scenes are routinely transformed into symbolic representations that ultimately become verbal language. However, the cognitive processes underlying this transformation remain only partially understood, largely because visual perception has traditionally been investigated through verbal descriptions that are already constrained by the grammatical organization of language. The present exploratory study proposes an alternative methodological approach by introducing pictogram-based representations as an intermediate level of conceptualization between visual perception and verbal description.
Twenty-four native speakers of Puerto Rican Spanish viewed three experimentally designed visual scenes while their eye movements were recorded using Gazepoint GP3 eye tracker. Immediately afterward, participants described each scene first using pictograms and subsequently through verbal language. 
Qualitative inspection of scan paths revealed substantial variability in visual exploration across participants. In contrast, pictogram selections exhibited considerably greater convergence, suggesting that symbolic representations were not simple reproductions of gaze trajectories. 
Rather than demonstrating the existence of a visual grammar, the present study proposes a methodological framework for investigating how visual scenes become conceptual and symbolic representations before they are fully organized by linguistic structures. The findings suggest that pictogram-based representations may constitute an informative intermediate level for studying systematic visual organization at the vision–language interface.

articles.title: How and for Whom Do Perinatal Depression Interventions Work in LMICs? A Causal Inference and Machine Learning Analysis of Socioeconomic and Psychosocial Drivers
articles.authors: Nadine Seward; Alexis Elias; Wen Wei Loh; Ahmed Waqas; Ricardo Araya; Angus MacBeth; Emily Garman; Kimberley A. Goldsmith; Oye Gureje; Lola Kola
articles.abstract:
Background: Randomised trials evaluating psychological interventions for perinatal depression (PND) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) frequently provide conflicting findings. To optimise global maternal mental health interventions, we applied robust causal inference and causal machine learning approaches to individual participant data (IPD) to identify underlying causal mechanisms and responsive subgroups.
Methods: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from inception to November 19, 2025, for trials assessing the effectiveness of psychological interventions to treat PND. Using IPD, we assessed treatment effect heterogeneity using causal forests, and evaluated causal mechanisms using interventional effects for individual trials and across relevant pooled datasets.
Findings: Seven of 11 eligible studies provided IPD, yielding a pooled sample of 3,154 participants (1,700 intervention, 1,454 control). Heterogeneity analyses of all trials demonstrated top responders presented with higher baseline depression and lower education. A four-study subset incorporating social determinants revealed those with lower perceived social support and education responded best. This four-study subset comprised two two-trial subsets: one delivered by community health workers (CHWs) and one by peers. In the CHW-delivered subset, top responders were similar to the four-study subset; however, within the peer-delivered subset, this effect was negligible. Causal mediation analyses of the four trials revealed social support mediated a 15% symptom reduction. The two-trial CHW subset indicated social support and reduced food insecurity mediated 15% and 3% improvements, respectively. Furthermore, a specific two-trial subset indicated behavioural activation and social support mediated improvements of 32% and 17%.
Interpretation: Despite interventions effectively targeting perceived social support, trials capturing food insecurity demonstrated minimal impact. The failure of peer-delivered interventions to reach vulnerable women, unlike CHW-delivered trials, suggests highly disadvantaged populations benefit least from a lower-cadre workforce. Optimising global maternal mental health requires assertively targeting socioeconomic determinants such as food insecurity and deploying CHWs to support the most vulnerable populations.

articles.title: Beyond the Microbiome: Neuroimaging and the Role of Gut Motility in Gut-Brain Interactions
articles.authors: Zeynep Ertürk; Klara Nielsen; Leah Banellis; Henrik M. Roager; Anke Ninija Karabanov
articles.abstract: Bidirectional communication between the gut and the brain has emerged as a major research focus in recent years, accompanied by increasing use of neuroimaging approaches to investigate how variation in gut microbial composition relates to brain activity, connectivity, and behavior in humans.  In contrast, significantly less human neuroimaging data has examined how the brain contributes to regulation and perception of gastrointestinal motility.  Recently, a growing body of work has begun to investigate how gastric motility relates to neural dynamics in humans. This review aims to address this emerging area by providing a comprehensive overview of experimental approaches that use neuroimaging to quantify the relationship between gut motility, brain activity, and behavior. Specifically, we review three complementary experimental approaches for investigating the role of gut motility in gut–brain interactions: (i) neuroimaging studies comparing dysregulated and healthy gut motility, (ii) perturbation paradigms targeting gastrointestinal signaling pathways, and (iii) studies examining functional coupling between gastrointestinal rhythms and brain activity. Finally, we discuss key open questions and methodological gaps and outline future directions for advancing mechanistic insight into gut–brain signalling.

articles.title: Designing Digital Games to Foster Growth Mindset in PreK–12 Education: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Seyedahmad Rahimi; Salah Esmaeiligoujar; Deniz Ercan; Ran Gao; Supharoek Keawphonkrang
articles.abstract:
Background: A growth mindset refers to the belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through effort, learning, and persistence. Although digital games are often associated with motivational and learning benefits, little is known about how they are intentionally designed to foster growth mindset in preK–12 learners. Understanding how growth mindset principles are operationalized within game mechanics and learning environments is critical for advancing both theory and practice in serious game design.
Purpose: This systematic review synthesizes how digital games have been designed and implemented to promote growth mindset in preK–12 education and examines associated student outcomes and future research directions.
Method: Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 2,063 records across multiple databases and included 12 empirical studies that explicitly integrated growth-mindset-supportive design elements into digital games. Data were extracted and analyzed to identify trends in study design, targeted competencies, reported effects, and specific game design features.
Results: Most reviewed studies reported positive effects on growth mindset and related competencies (e.g., persistence, creativity, self-efficacy), although some showed mixed or non-significant effects linked to design quality or implementation context. Two overarching design categories emerged: direct supports (e.g., explicit mindset instruction and effort-based rewards) and indirect supports (e.g., adaptive challenges, scaffolding, and mastery-oriented gameplay).
Conclusion: Well-designed digital games hold promise for fostering growth mindset in preK–12 contexts. However, the evidence base remains limited, highlighting the need for more rigorous research designs, longer-term interventions, and deeper theoretical integration to inform scalable and effective game-based mindset interventions.

articles.title: Cross-linguistic Semantic Stability as a Driving Force of Diachronic Semantic Evolution across Lexica
articles.authors: Liu Yufeng; Xingyu Yang
articles.abstract: Word meanings change over time, yet the rate of this change varies systematically within each lexicon. While frequency, age of acquisition, and concreteness have been identified as within-language predictors of semantic change rate, a language-general account of why some concepts resist diachronic drift more persistently than others worldwide has remained elusive. Here, we propose that cross-linguistic semantic stability — the degree to which a concept’s semantic neighborhood is conserved across languages — functions as a fundamental, conceptual-level constraint on diachronic semantic evolution across lexica. We operationalized semantic stability as neighborhood overlap between a target concept’s nearest neighbors in English and the back-translated neighbors of its translation equivalents across 10-to-41 languages, and quantified diachronic semantic change as neighborhood turnover in historical embeddings spanning up to 100 years in English, French, German, and Chinese. Concepts with higher cross-linguistic stability exhibited significantly slower diachronic semantic change within each language and, critically, across lexica when datasets were aggregated cross-linguistically to derive concepts’ change rates. This constraining effect dominated all other predictors for shared concepts; survived controls for well-established psycholinguistic predictors; was structurally confirmed through partial-correlation networks as a direct, unmediated constraint; remained robust under iterative sample expansion of cross-lingual concept sets; and was replicated using historically derived stability estimates. Altogether, our findings reveal that the topological consistency of a concept’s semantic neighborhood across the world’s languages reflects a temporally durable cognitive-communicative constraint that actively governs the pace of meaning change, bridging synchronic cross-linguistic aligned conceptual structure with the diachronic dynamics of lexical evolution across lexica.

articles.title: Differential modulation of temporal precision and perceived timing by tactile spatial and temporal context
articles.authors: Mehdi Adibi
articles.abstract: Perception of sensory events depends not only on the stimulus itself but also on the surrounding spatial and temporal context. While contextual interactions have been extensively studied in vision, less is known about how tactile spatial and temporal context shape temporal representation of tactile landmarks embedded within continuous tactile signals. we investigated how neighbouring tactile stimuli influence the temporal precision and perceived timing of a target tactile landmark using an auditory-referenced temporal order judgement task. The number, location, and relative timing of task-irrelevant vibrotactile flankers were manipulated independently. Increasing the number of flankers reduced temporal precision, with comparable effects for adjacent and contralateral stimulation, indicating that temporal precision is limited by contextual interactions beyond local spatial proximity. In contrast, the relative timing of the flankers did not alter temporal sensitivity but systematically shifted perceived target timing. Flankers preceding the target shifted the perceived timing of the target earlier, whereas lagging flankers shifted it to the opposite direction. When one flanker preceded and the other followed the target the direction of the resulting spatiotemporal sequence across the fingers determined the direction of the perceptual bias. These findings reveal two distinct forms of contextual modulation in tactile temporal perception. Spatial context degrades temporal precision, whereas temporal context shifts perceived event timing. These findings demonstrate that spatial and temporal context shape distinct temporal aspects of tactile representations, extending contextual interference from feature identity and localisation to temporal precision and perceived timing.

articles.title: Linearity-preserving scores for general measurement errors
articles.authors: Mathias Berggren
articles.abstract: A model of how errors-in-variables measurements with a certain expectation structure preserves linear relationship between latent error-free variables is presented (Theorem 1). This also allows a simple relationship between latent and observed explained variances through the variance that remains in the measurements (Corollary 2). The resulting model can be applied to a broad set of measurement issues and provides the outline for a novel Expectation-minimization (Em) algorithm (Theorem 2) for latent linear regression (SEM) estimation under various error structures. The method is illustrated by an application to tetrachoric correlations and to an applied example incorporating prior information into the estimation.

articles.title: Pathways to Economic Flourishing: A Positive Economic Psychology Model of Financial Wellbeing
articles.authors: Rona Hart; Dan Hart
articles.abstract:
This paper presents a novel model of financial wellbeing grounded in the principles of Positive Economic Psychology, an emerging interdisciplinary field that integrates insights from Positive Psychology and Economic Psychology to promote economic prosperity and optimal economic functioning in individuals, groups, and institutions. 
The proposed model is grounded in two theories: Hope Theory  and the Transtheoretical Model of Behaviour Change. It positions financial wellbeing as a hierarchical construct that offers pathways to financial wellbeing.  At its foundation are individuals’ dispositions and financial outlooks, which provide the bedrock for financial growth. The second tier concerns financial literacy and skills, which are essential for informed financial decision-making and the maximisation of opportunities. These  underpin the third tier: decisions and planning. The fourth tier refers to social context and social responsibility  guiding principles that influences financial decisions and behaviours. The fifth tier  includes financial behaviours, representing the application of a positive mindset, effective knowledge, skills and decisions towards achieving and maintaining financial wellbeing. At the top of the hierarchy are accomplishments, representing the ultimate expression and outcomes of effective financial behaviours. This final tier centres on the attainment of financial goals and the achievement of a secure and satisfying financial state. Situated outside the hierarchy are contextual and sociodemographic factors that can influence each tier and should be considered at every stage in the pursuit of financial wellbeing. The paper also reviews other models of financial wellbeing as well as the research evidence supporting the model.

articles.title: Partner Responsiveness and Insensitivity Predict Emotion Regulation Flexibility in Parent-Adolescent Dyads: A Daily Diary Investigation
articles.authors: Dunja Tutus; Reuma Gadassi Polack; Jutta Joormann; Ann-Christin Haag
articles.abstract: This study examined how perceived partner responsiveness (PPR) and insensitivity (PPI) predict daily emotion regulation (ER) flexibility, operationalized via the maladaptive ER ratio. Adolescents (N = 112, 12–18 years) and caregivers (N = 108, 33–64 years) dyads completed 28-day diaries. Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) analyses showed that actor (between and within person) PPR predicted higher ER flexibility, whereas actor PPI predicted lower ER flexibility (ps < .038). Partner higher daily PPR predicted higher ER flexibility (p = .040). Furthermore, role (adolescent/caregiver) moderated the actor daily PPR effect (p = .037) and the partner daily PPI effect (p = .007), revealing distinct relational daily dynamics across roles. These findings highlight how interpersonal attachment perceptions shape daily family ER flexibility.

articles.title: Concurrent and Lagged Synchrony in Parents’ and Adolescents’ Daily Positive and Negative Affect: Distinct Predictors Across Synchrony Types
articles.authors: Hannah E. Marshall; Haran Sened; Kelley Gunther; Jutta Joormann; Reuma Gadassi Polack
articles.abstract: Most research on parent–adolescent emotion dynamics has relied on brief laboratory paradigms, which provide limited insight into whether affective synchrony unfolds in everyday life and what factors drive its patterns. In this pre-registered study, a community sample (69.5% Caucasian, 10.9% Black, 7.3% Bi/Multiracial, 12.3% other races) of 112 adolescents (M = 14.13 years, SD = 1.74, Range = 12–18; 61 female, 49 male, 2 nonbinary) and 108 of their parents (M = 43.98 years, SD = 6.00, Range = 33–64; 96 female, 12 male) completed baseline measures of closeness, responsiveness, insensitivity, depressive symptoms, and social anxiety symptoms. Then, for 28 days, participants reported their positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA). We used Bayesian LMEM to quantify concurrent synchrony in PA and NA and test whether baseline measures predicted each type of synchrony. Results confirmed that parents and adolescents exhibited concurrent synchrony in their daily PA (β = 0.228) and NA (β = 0.278). Concurrent synchrony in PA and NA were differentially predicted by adolescents’ (but usually not parents’) perceptions of their relationship and social anxiety symptoms. Exploratory analyses examining lagged synchrony evidenced similar effects. In addition to advancing theoretical understanding of parent–adolescent emotion dynamics, these findings suggest that the dissociability of positive and negative emotions may extend to dyadic affective processes.

articles.title: Registered Reports Reduce Bias and Improve Trust in Machine Learning
articles.authors: Kristin Jankowsky; Kim-Laura Speck; Jamie Cummins; Ulrich Schroeders
articles.abstract: We propose the use of Registered Reports in applied machine learning research to strengthen methodological rigor, constrain researcher degrees of freedom, and better harness the potential of machine learning. We outline the main requirements for successful implementation and highlight the key benefits of this proposal.

articles.title: Mouse cursor tracking contributes to the psychological validation of the drift diffusion model
articles.authors: Oliver Grenke; Stefan Scherbaum; Martin Schoemann
articles.abstract: As a well-established cognitive model of human decision-making, the drift diffusion model (DDM) offers a psychologically intuitive account of the decision-making process by virtue of its four basic parameters. However, the reliance of the DDM on endpoint measures (response times and accuracy) creates a conceptual gap to this process-oriented account, which needs to be bridged with the help of independent process-tracing methods. In this study, we deployed mouse cursor tracking with the aim of validating the psychological interpretation of the basic DDM parameters drift rate, threshold separation, and non-decision time.  In a preregistered replication, 95 participants completed 90 trials of a random dot kinematogram (RDK). Partial least square regression was applied in order to predict the three DDM parameters with the help of 18 cursor measures, which were extracted from the literature. We found support for the psychological interpretation of threshold separation and non-decision time, replicating the results of our previous study, while the analyses of drift rate remained inconclusive. Our results further strengthen our psychological understanding of the DDM, point towards conceptual ambiguities, and encourage further joint application of cognitive models and process-tracing methodology.

articles.title: A Two-Stage Scaffolding Model of Color and Luminance Development: Retinal Waves, Global Impoverishment, and Luminance-Grounded Object Representations
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: How does the visual system construct object representations that are robust to the removal of color? I propose a two-stage scaffolding model. In Stage 1 (prenatal), retinal waves establish spectrally non-selective spatiotemporal contrast sensitivity, the necessary structural foundation of the visual system, before any visual experience occurs. Because the wave-generating circuitry encodes only contrasts in firing rate with no access to spectral information, this foundation is necessarily achromatic: whatever circuits retinal waves entrain, they are trained on a signal that carries no chromatic content. In Stage 2 (postnatal), the globally degraded neonatal visual signal, low spatial resolution, low contrast sensitivity, and immature chromatic processing, all coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity, forces the first object representations to be built on luminance structure, the only dimension with sufficient fidelity under maximal front-end degradation. Together, these two stages explain why normal observers recognize objects in grayscale as readily as in color: luminance structure was the foundation of object representations from the beginning. The model also explains why late-sighted individuals who gain sight after dense congenital cataracts show disproportionate reliance on color: they retain the prenatal structural scaffold (intact retinas generating normal retinal waves) but lack the postnatal experiential scaffold (years of globally impoverished visual experience that normally grounds object representations in luminance). The model generates testable predictions that distinguish it from color-specific developmental accounts, and several can be evaluated on existing computational architectures without new patient data.

articles.title: Toward a Formalization of Human Intuitive Theories of Bodily Pain
articles.authors: Marlene Berke; Katherine M Collins; Joshua Tenenbaum; Rebecca Saxe
articles.abstract: Pain is a private, subjective experience, yet observers routinely make consequential judgments about another person’s pain (e.g., whether it warrants treatment, accommodation, or whether it’s real at all). How do observers make these judgments? We propose that people attribute pain through an intuitive theory—the same kind of theory they use to infer other hidden mental and physical states. We explore the structure of people’s intuitive theory of pain by formalizing competing conceptions of pain: from pain resulting from bodily damage observable through physical evidence to pain as a subjective experience known only via self-report. Each theory is formalized as a causal model that predicts how people interpret naturalistic vignettes drawn from Reddit posts and medical training materials. Three experiments probe classical signatures of Bayesian causal reasoning: predicting pain from physical evidence (Experiment 1), inferring and treating pain (Experiment 2), and inferring a hidden cause (ulterior motives) that explains away inflated pain reports (Experiment 3). Across all three, a causal model that integrates over physical and mental states best captures human behavior and generalizes across eight categories of bodily pain, from headaches to finger burns. These results are consistent with our proposal that people have an intuitive theory of pain arising from problems in the body, and this theory supports quantitative causal reasoning. As a direct consequence of this intuitive theory, lay people view pain reports that lack corroborating physical evidence with suspicion. This work is a first step toward a quantitative, scientific model of folk intuitive theories of pain.

articles.title: Online Behavioral Experiments with jsPsych: A Workflow Guide
articles.authors: Moritz Schiltenwolf; Mario Gollwitzer
articles.abstract: Online behavioral experiments have become increasingly common due to advances in web technologies and the availability of browser-based experimental frameworks. Among these, jsPsych has emerged as a widely used JavaScript library that allows researchers to implement behavioral experiments directly in web browsers. Despite its flexibility and extensive functionality, developing experiments with jsPsych can be challenging for researchers with limited programming experience. This paper introduces a structured workflow for creating online experiments with jsPsych. The workflow decomposes experiment development into four conceptual steps: 1) Defining experimental conditions and their dependencies; 2) Designing the structure of individual trials; 3) Integrating functional elements such as instructions and questionnaires; 4) Assembling the complete experiment timeline. The practical application of the workflow is illustrated through three fully runnable example implementations: a Stroop task, an Eriksen Flanker task, and an Immediate Serial Recall task. The first example closely follows the four-step workflow as presented in this paper, whereas the second and third examples retain the same underlying workflow while adopting a more general and modular code structure that separates reusable functionality from experiment-specific configurations. These examples highlight how structured programming approaches can simplify experiment development and code reusability, thereby contributing to an improvement in code reproducibility by other researchers.

articles.title: Mapping psychological processes governing the sociopolitical climate system
articles.authors: Madalina Vlasceanu; Sara Madureira Constantino
articles.abstract: Climate change is often treated as a technological or environmental challenge, yet societal responses are shaped by the psychological and sociopolitical dynamics linking institutions, markets, and human behavior. Existing research has largely examined climate governance and individual psychological processes in isolation. Here we propose a multi-actor psychological systems (MAPS) model of climate action that integrates these perspectives by mapping influence pathways among seven key actors (i.e., researchers, civil society, policymakers, elites, industry, media, and the public) and identifying the processes mediating these relationships. These actors influence the sociopolitical climate system through mechanisms such as science communication, agenda setting, activism, lobbying, consumer behavior, and electoral politics. We argue that psychological processes, including risk perception, social norms, social identity, elite cueing, motivated reasoning, moral values, efficacy beliefs, and emotional processes, mediate many of these relationships and help explain why scientific knowledge does not consistently translate into policy adoption or behavioral change. By linking micro-level psychological mechanisms with macro-level institutional dynamics through the focus on these seven key actors, the MAPS framework clarifies how climate action emerges, or stalls, within complex sociopolitical systems and highlights leverage points for interventions that could accelerate climate mitigation and societal transformation.

articles.title: Multimodal Signals of Multiparty Audience Design in Moderate-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: Divergent Patterns in Spoken Language, Gesture, and Eye Gaze
articles.authors: Sharice Clough; Sophia Kekes-Szabo; Melissa J Evans; Marianne Casilio; Sarah Brown-Schmidt; Melissa Collins Duff
articles.abstract:
Background: Multiparty communication challenges speakers to adapt their messages for multiple addressees with varying knowledge levels. Such studies of multiparty audience design in both typical and clinical populations have narrowly focused on spoken language only. In the current study, we extend this analysis to examine how speakers with and without TBI adapt their gesture and eye gaze behaviors for multiparty audience design. 
Method: 30 adults with moderate-severe TBI and 30 non-injured participants played a referential communication game with two Matchers. In the Sorting phase, they described abstract images repeatedly across four rounds. In a subsequent Test phase, participants described the images again to groups of two Matchers who were either both knowledgeable, both naïve, or mixed. We used video-based motion tracking to quantify adaptations in gesture form kinematics for groups of listeners with different levels of knowledge and manually annotated gaze events toward Matchers. 
Results: Non-injured participants demonstrated a coordinated effort for multiparty audience design across modalities, maximizing the informativeness of their spoken and gestural descriptions and using gaze to monitor understanding in naïve and mixed group conditions. In contrast, despite showing reduced adaptation in spoken language, participants with TBI showed preserved adaptation in kinematic features of gesture form and appropriately allocated gaze to naïve Matchers, signaling awareness of partner-specific knowledge representations. Participants with TBI produced gestures at significantly higher rates than non-injured peers.  
Conclusions: The results highlight the importance of a multimodal approach to studying cognitive-communication disorders and new insights into cognitive mechanisms underlying disruptions to multiparty audience design.

articles.title: Multiparty Audience Design is Disrupted following Moderate-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: Evidence of Reduced Spoken Language Adjustment
articles.authors: Sophia Kekes-Szabo; Melissa J Evans; Marianne Casilio; Sarah Brown-Schmidt; Melissa Collins Duff; Sharice Clough
articles.abstract:
Background: Social communication impairments after traumatic brain injury (TBI) affect a range of skills required for effective conversation. We examined how adults with TBI adjust their communication when speaking to multiple communication partners with variable shared knowledge (i.e., multiparty audience design).
Method: 30 adults with moderate-severe TBI and 30 non-injured comparison (NC) participants played a referential communication game to assess multiparty audience design. In the Sorting phase, participants (the “Director”), described abstract images to two trained research assistant “Matchers” who sorted the same images in a matching order. They sorted the images four times, establishing shared labels for the images. In a later Test phase, we manipulated Matcher knowledge across three conditions: participants described the images again to groups of two Matchers who were either a) both knowledgeable about the image labels, b) both naïve, or c) mixed. We examined participants’ adjustments in expression length, definite reference, and disfluency across Sorting phase rounds and Test phase conditions.
Results: In the Sorting phase, the TBI group showed reduced gains in referential efficiency over the four rounds of the game compared to non-injured peers. At Test phase, the TBI group significantly adjusted their spoken language for groups with one or more naïve listeners (i.e., longer expressions, more disfluencies, and fewer definite references), but the magnitude of these effects was significantly smaller than the NC group.
Conclusions: Participants with TBI showed reduced spoken language adjustment for multiparty audience design, increasing risk for disruptions in navigating group communication in work, school, and interpersonal relationships.

articles.title: WEIRD Questions: Diversifying Conceptual Sampling
articles.authors: Mohammad Atari; Ivan Kroupin; Liora Morhayim; Damián E. Blasi; Jonathan Friedemann Schulz; Joseph Henrich
articles.abstract: Psychological science is defined in terms of the study of the human mind. Psychological research, however, has fallen short of examining diverse human populations, with most existing research focused on a small slice of human diversity around the globe, typically people from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) populations. On top of the WEIRD-participants problem, there is also a bias in the researchers themselves, most of whom come from WEIRD backgrounds. Here, we make the case for a new and distinct source of bias: WEIRD questions. Our species offers a substantially varied distribution of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral repertoires, but researchers have sampled topics and questions from a small part of this distribution, leaving out a variety of cognitive processes, emotions, and behaviors that remain understudied. We review sources of bias in asking questions about the human mind, discuss examples, and call for diversifying conceptual sampling in psychological science. We close by discussing some remedies to counter the WEIRD-questions problem: taking theory seriously, valuing descriptive research, rethinking team science, and aligning structural disciplinary incentives.

articles.title: Repetition Learning Depends on the Explicit Retrieval from Episodic Memory: Evidence from EEG
articles.authors: Philipp Musfeld; Keisuke Fukuda
articles.abstract: A classic demonstration of long-term learning by repetition is the Hebb effect: immediate recall improves for memory sets presented repeatedly amidst non-repeated sets. Although long regarded as a form of implicit learning, recent work combining individual-participant analysis with computational modeling has shown that learning emerges only after participants become aware of the repetition. The reminding account of the Hebb effect explains these recent findings by proposing that repetition learning requires retrieving a prior encounter of the repeated material from episodic memory during re-encoding; repetitions that go unrecognized are encoded as novel episodes and produce no learning. Here, we tested this explanation using EEG. Participants performed a visual working memory task on 150 visual arrays per block, two of which recurred every ~5th trial. During the task, we measured recall performance, trial-by-trial repetition awareness, and EEG during encoding of arrays. Behaviorally, we replicate that learning of repeated arrays emerged only after participants recognized their repetition. At the neural level, the late positive component (LPC), an established marker of episodic recollection, was enhanced for repeated relative to novel arrays — but only after recognition, and already before recall improved. In contrast, the FN400, an index of familiarity, and a whole-scalp topographic analysis revealed no difference between unrecognized repeated and novel arrays, indicating that unrecognized repetitions are processed like new information. We conclude that repetition learning in the Hebb paradigm is gated not by the gradual, implicit accumulation of experience, but by the explicit retrieval of prior encounters from episodic memory at reencoding.

articles.title: (A)I wrote this for you: Memory for presumably AI-generated and human-written prose
articles.authors: Maria Falikman; Louise Ferguson; Hieu Phan; Karissa Allmon; Allison Craft; Aidan Ganchan; Tianning Lyu; Abduldayam Maflahi; Marlin Price; Grace Stevens
articles.abstract: The exponential rise of artificial intelligence-generated content in recent years has raised questions about how humans process, remember, and recall information based on its assumed source. Our study examined whether labeled authorship affects memory recall by testing the hypothesis that memory for human-authored text would be superior to memory for text believed to be generated by a large language model (LLM). A total of 122 undergraduate college students were randomly assigned to read identical excerpts of contemporary American prose labeled as either human-authored or AI-generated, then completed a surprise memory test along with measures of recall confidence and text readability, likability, and engagement. We observed higher memory recall in participants who believed they were reading a passage written by a human author, while participants who thought the story was written by an LLM recalled significantly fewer details. Participants also reported significantly higher engagement with a human-attributed text, though engagement did not correlate with memory performance. These findings suggest that perceived authorship influences memory recall independently of subjective engagement, with implications for understanding human-AI interactions in educational contexts.

articles.title: Benchmarking Relational Safety in Empathic AI: Perceived Empathy and Relational Appropriateness Can Diverge Across Large Language Models
articles.authors: Lauren Ministero
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for emotional support, and a growing body of work suggests that these systems can produce responses that are rated as more empathic than those of highly trained humans. Far less attention has been paid to whether these empathic responses are also relationally appropriate, meaning whether they maintain suitable boundaries, avoid fostering dependency, and support rather than substitute for users' own coping and social resources. The present study separates perceived empathy from relational appropriateness and tests whether these two dimensions diverge across large language models. Forty naturalistic, emotionally vulnerable prompts were submitted to the flagship model from four major providers (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Llama 4 Maverick), yielding 160 responses that were rated by two trained coders on validated empathy items and a novel relational appropriateness scale developed for this work. Perceived empathy and relational appropriateness were both highly reliable and unidimensional, but they related to one another differently across models (F(3, 112) = 4.39, p = .006). For most models, higher perceived empathy was associated with higher appropriateness, but for one (Llama 4 Maverick) this relationship was flat to slightly negative. Qualitative examples illustrate how a response can be rated as highly empathic while simultaneously discouraging external help-seeking and positioning the AI as a relational substitute. These findings suggest that empathy and relational appropriateness are separable constructs that should be evaluated independently, and that psychologists should be involved in the design of empathic AI safeguards.

articles.title: Techno-optimistic scientists take fewer climate actions
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Viktoria Cologna; Maien Sachisthal; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Technological innovation is key to mitigating climate change, yet excessive faith in technology may undermine the wider societal transformations needed to address it. In their roles as knowledge producers and trusted public figures, scientists play a vital part in shaping how societies understand and respond to climate change. We examine techno-optimism — here defined as the belief that technology will largely solve the problems caused by climate change — among scientists using survey data from N = 9,199 scientists across 115 countries. Our findings show that techno-optimism is most prevalent among scientists in applied and natural sciences, and among those with right-leaning political views. Techno-optimistic scientists are substantially less likely to engage in civic climate action (28% lower) or make high-impact lifestyle changes (20% lower).
