How much of their views people convey at a time is thus a distinct lever shaping where discussions go.

articles.title: Fiscal Federalism in Argentina, Revisited: The Dangling Thread of Municipal Governance
articles.authors: Jorge Gordin; Emilia Simison
articles.abstract: In many respects, Argentina is an antithetic case of fiscal federalism. Challenging established theses on the benefits of decentralized revenue responsibilities, its fiscal governance predicates predominantly on central government´s dominance. While significant research efforts were undertaken to decipher the roots of the resulting fiscal centralization, there is a shortage of analyses exploring the role of municipal governments in this theoretical puzzle. This chapter seeks to rectify such omission, underscoring the paramount function of municipal governments as grassroots carriers of federal fiscal governance. It begins with a discussion of the theoretical state-of-the-art on local politics in federalism studies, in general, and Argentina, in particular. Next, we take a snapshot at the demographic and economic data of local governments and municipal regimes in Argentina, identifying their historical and structural underpinnings. Third, we turn our attention to the evolution and consequences of local fiscal empowerment since the 1994 Constitutional Reform. Fourth, it examines the effects and results of local governance in decisive policy areas to assess the extent to which it can be considered a critical missing link of nation-province relationships. In closing, we claim that despite significant strides were accomplished in advancing political decentralization in the wake of the 1994 Constitutional Reform, deepening national, provincial, and municipal triadic fiscal relations stands out as a pending assignment for further consolidating federal rule in the country.

articles.title: Hidden Labor, Hidden Harm: Gendered Trauma and the Paradox of Double Exposure in Federal Probation
articles.authors: Sandra L. Trappen; Ethan Michael Galley; Cristina Figueroa; Bobur Rakhmatullaev
articles.abstract: This U.S.-based study examines how hierarchical structures organize the emotional and relational labor of federal probation officers, shaping the institutional conditions under which justice work occurs. Drawing on a national survey of 423 officers and in‑depth interviews with 30 participants, we show how expectations of composure, distributions of relational work, and organizational norms that discourage strain disclosure create patterned vulnerabilities across the workforce. Officers in frontline roles, particularly women of color and men of color, report heightened demands and scrutiny, revealing how institutional cultures distribute emotional labor and constrain expressions of strain. Qualitative accounts illuminate the paradox of double exposure: officers are both survivors of trauma and practitioners managing others’ trauma within environments that reward stoicism and limit vulnerability. Strain emerges as the operational expression of structurally produced trauma, underscoring that trauma‑informed justice must begin with the workforce.

articles.title: The Occupational Trauma Compounding Model: Structural Selection and the Deepening of Psychological Harm in the U.S. Service Industry
articles.authors: Alyson Williams
articles.abstract: The U.S. service industry employs nearly 17 million people and is disproportionately populated by individuals with histories of early adversity, yet no single framework connects the scattered evidence on this workforce across occupational health psychology, trauma psychology, labor economics, and addiction research. This paper advances the Occupational Trauma Compounding Model (OTCM), an integrative theoretical account arguing that the industry structurally selects for trauma-exposed workers and then compounds psychological harm through occupational, physiological, and legal mechanisms, with a distinct symptom picture that persists after workers exit. The model is organized across four levels: (1) structural and psychological selection; (2) occupational entrenchment through trauma bonding, coworker identity fusion, harassment and violence, and the legal exploitation of salaried managers; (3) physiological compounding via substance use, sleep disruption, and nutritional deficiency; and (4) post-industry sequelae that existing diagnostic frameworks systematically misclassify. The paper situates the model against the dominant occupational-stress frameworks — job demands–resources, demand–control, and effort–reward imbalance — and against the burnout construct, arguing that the OTCM adds a selection layer beneath them, an attachment mechanism within them, and a persistence claim beyond them. Synthesizing evidence across published literatures and national datasets, the paper specifies twelve falsifiable propositions and the study designs that would test them, addresses the central identification problem of separating selection from causation, and outlines clinical and policy implications. Primary survey data collection is underway. The OTCM is offered as a testable research agenda for an under-recognized population.

articles.title: Environmental Conservation or the Treadmill of Law: A Case Study of the Post-2014 Husbandry Waste Regulations in China
articles.authors: KuoRayMao; Shuqin Jin; Yu Hu; Nefratiri Weeks; Liangjun Ye
articles.abstract: As industrialized animal agriculture expanded rapidly in the last decade, the resultant pollution has generated widespread despoliation of natural resources and environmental victimization in rural China. This study examines the formulation and implementation of national environmental regulations from 2014 to 2019 and finds that the juxtaposing ministerial and provincial jurisdictions resulted in conflicting interpretations of the scale and evaluation criteria of the national policy. We argue that the regulations are more than centralized conservation programs designed to reduce environmental pollution caused by the expansion of animal husbandry. Instead, these regulations are fundamentally state-led rural development initiatives that utilize the designations of ecological protection zones to reconfigure land use and promote scale-up production in agricultural structural adjustment initiatives. The enforcement of these environmental regulations, therefore, constitutes a treadmill of law (ToL) that accelerated the geographical specialization and function intensification of the Chinese husbandry sector.

articles.title: Constrained Agency under Existential Threat: Immigrant Entrepreneurship and Expulsion
articles.authors: Robertson Khan Tengeh
articles.abstract: Structural and socio-cultural constraints have long shaped African immigrant entrepreneurship in South Africa. The organised anti-foreigner campaigns of 2025–2026 echoed the earlier expulsions in Ghana (1969) and Nigeria (1983). What made them different was that the host society itself became the organised source of existential threat. This article aimed to develop a theoretical framework accounting for how entrepreneurial agency changes when organised political mobilisation simultaneously threatens physical safety, legal presence, and venture survival. The framework was developed as a conceptual model by drawing on constrained agency theory alongside scholarship on institutions, social movements, scapegoating, and moral panic. Rather than being tested with primary data, it was illustrated through historical and contemporary African cases. CAT-ET suggests that when constraints become existential, agency tends to shift towards either adaptive persistence or strategic exit. Two interacting mechanisms were specified: functional institutional inaccessibility under violence, whereby protective institutions remained operational but selectively inaccessible, and the entrepreneur-as-symbol dynamic, whereby immigrant ventures became politically constructed as emblems of economic grievance. CAT-ET reframed organised expulsion as a recurring political-economic process and offered a basis for comparative research across the Global South.

articles.title: A Blended Distribution
articles.authors: George Y. Nie
articles.abstract: We use an example to show that a distribution is asymmetric generally, arguing that a distribution in the real word is totally different from a normal distribution. Treating the force behind asymmetry as momentum, we define a distribution with momentum as a blended distribution—as if a normal distribution is disfigured by, or blended with, momentum. We propose that a variable’s movement over a period follows a distribution longitudinally whereas the literature is usually limited to a variable’s population that follows a distribution cross-sectionally. We show how the distribution of observations indicates the likelihood at a time that the variable falls within a range.

articles.title: Governing AI in Viet Nam: Centralised digital sovereignty and controlled interdependence
articles.authors: THI NGOC ANH NGUYEN
articles.abstract: In debates on digital sovereignty, states seek to build the technological and regulatory capacity to govern dependence on foreign digital infrastructures. AI complicates this ambition because its development relies on globally concentrated chips, cloud services, foundation models, capital and technical expertise. This article examines how Viet Nam seeks to build domestic AI capability while remaining integrated into global technology markets. Drawing on qualitative document analysis of Viet Nam’s legal and policy instruments, together with records of foreign AI and infrastructure partnerships, the article conceptualises Viet Nam’s approach as developmental digital sovereignty through controlled interdependence. Viet Nam combines risk-based AI regulation, national AI and data infrastructure, public support for domestic innovation and strategic coordination of technology development with continued foreign investment, research partnerships and technology cooperation. The analysis identifies a non-exclusionary variant of centralised digital sovereignty in which state coordination over infrastructure, data and regulation coexists with continuing foreign participation. It finds stronger evidence of policy aspiration and regulatory access than of material leverage over critical chips, cloud infrastructure or models. However, this strategy remains politically ambiguous. The institutions intended to strengthen domestic compute, data and research capacity also centralise regulatory authority, expand executive discretion and provide limited publicly visible mechanisms for independent oversight. The article argues that developmental digital sovereignty should be assessed through both its capacity to reshape external technological dependence and the accountability conditions governing the domestic exercise of technological power.

articles.title: From 4-Digit Codes to Social Class: Benchmarking Supervised Classification, Semantic Retrieval, and LLM Reranking for Multilingual Occupational Coding and Downstream Stratification (Technical report: model design, evaluation, and derived-measure accuracy)
articles.authors: Erdem YILMAZ; Elias H. Kruithof; Pieter-Paul Verhaeghe
articles.abstract: This report documents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a fully local pipeline that codes multilingual free-text occupation responses into the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08) and derives from those codes the social-class and status measures (e.g., ESeC, ISEI, Oesch) on which much of stratification research depends. This coding is costly, slow, and only moderately consistent when done by hand. The pipeline is local (hence GDPR-friendly), reproducible, and runs on consumer-grade hardware. We benchmark and compare three approaches to the coding step: (M1) a supervised multilingual transformer classifier; (M2) semantic retrieval against a 361k-document multilingual occupation index; and (M3) the supervised classifier with an added large-language-model reranking step. On held-out European Social Survey (ESS) data the supervised classifier reaches 59.2% exact four-digit accuracy, comparable to human inter-coder agreement for this intrinsically ambiguous task, which is itself low at the four-digit level (reported by past research to be ≈42–53% between individual coders; κ ≈ 0.5 between agencies). More importantly for stratification research, given that coding errors are mostly near-misses that coarser schemes absorb, the sociologically relevant aggregate measures are recovered far more accurately, namely 80.4% for the 9-class ESeC (87.8% for its 5-class collapse), 80.5% for the 7-group ESeG, 77.9% for the 16-category Oesch scheme, and a Pearson correlation of 0.87 for the ISEI socio-economic index. The same class- and status-level accuracy holds when the model is trained and tested on canonical occupation text, so it is not an artefact of the ESS sample. Retrieval alone (M2) is substantially weaker, and contrary to the intuitive expectation, adding an LLM reranker (M3) reduces accuracy on noisy multilingual survey responses (−3.7 pp), while on clean canonical titles its effect is approximately neutral, i.e., +0.5 pp over the backbone it reranks, with no gain over the best supervised model. Instead, the supervised model’s (M1) well-calibrated confidence (ECE = 0.038) supports a human-in-the-loop workflow in which only genuinely uncertain cases are escalated to human coders. We report bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests for every comparison, a train/test leakage audit, and a decomposition of geographic variation showing that the cross-country accuracy spread (in the ESS corpus) reflects response style and occupational-title ambiguity rather than language resources, whereas a genuine resource effect appears only across languages on canonical text in the normative corpus. The pipeline runs entirely offline on a single consumer-grade workstation, making automated, auditable occupation coding feasible without sending respondent data to external services.

articles.title: Locke on Money and Trust:  Between Fides, Trusteeship, and Confidence
articles.authors: JHET Assistant; Tomas Lima Pimenta
articles.abstract: This paper reinterprets the money–trust nexus in John Locke by distinguishing three rationalities of trust at work across his moral, political, and monetary writings: fides, trusteeship (fiduciary power), and confidence. Against England’s monetary turmoil of the 1690s, it reads Locke’s monetary interventions as attempts to secure public faith and contractual stability amid monetary deterioration and contested proposals to ““raise” money’s value. Fides underwrites promising and the moral intelligibility of conventional signs yet remains too fragile to sustain monetary order without reliable sanctions. Trusteeship explains why fiduciary power can secure coining, standard maintenance, and the punishment of monetary crime, but cannot create value by decree. Finally, it tackles the puzzle of “intrinsick value” by reading Locke’s universal “consent of mankind” as confidence: an impersonal trust in the persistence of a social convention, neither natural essence nor sovereign fiat.

articles.title: Career Stability and Further Training for Workers with General versus Vocational Education
articles.authors: Viktor Decker; Marco Seegers
articles.abstract: The relative merits of vocational and general education remain central to debates on sustainable careers. Vocational pathways facilitate smoother labour market entry but risk skill obsolescence, whereas general education yields weaker entry prospects but greater adaptability. A key question is whether further training can offset these trade-offs. This study examines participation in, and career stability returns to, non-formal job-related training across educational tracks. General graduates are expected to benefit more in early careers, while vocational graduates should see higher stability returns later as training counteracts skill obsolescence. Drawing on the German National Educational Panel Study, the analysis shows that secondary-level vocational graduates participate less in training than university graduates, whereas tertiary-level vocational graduates train at similar rates. Training promotes employment stability in workers’ late careers, but effects are relatively uniform across educational groups. Given uniform returns, lower participation rates disadvantage secondary-level vocational graduates relative to workers with tertiary-level qualifications.

articles.title: JUSTFAIR 2.0: A public dataset linking U.S. federal criminal sentences to the individual judges who imposed them
articles.authors: Chad M. Topaz; Maria-Veronica Ciocanel; Zofia Stanley; Christopher Thomas; Katherine Durante
articles.abstract: Federal courts sentence tens of thousands of people every year, yet the public sentencing records released by the United States Sentencing Commission (USSC) deliberately omit the identity of the sentencing judge, limiting research on and public oversight of judicial discretion. We present JUSTFAIR 2.0, a public dataset that links 140,299 federal criminal sentencing records from fiscal years 2018 through 2023 to 969 individual district judges across 87 judicial districts, using only publicly available sources. We construct the dataset in three linkage stages: (1) linkage of USSC sentencing records to case records in the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database (FJCID) using a graph-based method with offense-code similarity scoring; (2) extraction of judge identifiers embedded in docket numbers scraped from the Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) system; and (3) matching of these identifiers to the Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges, which supplies each judge's full name, demographic information, appointment history, and appointing president. We validate the record linkage internally by comparing offense-code agreement between unique and non-unique matches (Jensen-Shannon divergence = 0.006) and validate judge matching by manually auditing a stratified sample of matches against PACER dockets, finding no errors. We document attrition at every pipeline stage and assess representativeness by comparing retained and excluded records on demographic, offense, and sentencing characteristics. The dataset updates and extends the original JUSTFAIR database, the first large-scale public resource connecting federal sentences to judges. We describe known structural limitations, including districts whose docket numbers lack judge identifiers, and offer guidance for appropriate use.

articles.title: Focused MAIHDA: Studying Intersectional Inequalities Through the Lens of a Focal Social Identity
articles.authors: George Leckie; Andrew Bell; Clare Evans
articles.abstract: Intersectional MAIHDA (Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy) is a widely used approach in quantitative intersectional research for examining inequalities across combinations of social identity characteristics, such as gender, race, and class. However, researchers often wish to center their analysis on a single social identity characteristic, such as gender, while preserving an intersectional analytical framework. This raises questions that existing MAIHDA models cannot directly address—for example, whether the magnitude or pattern of intersectional inequalities differs by gender. To address this limitation, we propose Focused MAIHDA, a multiple-equation extension that jointly estimates subgroup-specific MAIHDA models, enabling formal comparisons of intersectional inequalities across subgroups. In doing so, we expand the range of questions that MAIHDA can address and broaden its contribution to quantitative intersectional research. We motivate and illustrate our approach by revisiting the seminal application to body mass index (BMI) by Evans et al. (2018).

articles.title: Diagnosing social norms and their influence on adolescent girls’ experience of menstruation in Khulna, Bangladesh: A theory-led qualitative exploration
articles.authors: Heather Suttor; Tasfiyah Jalil; Arifa Bente Mohosin; Erin C Hunter; Abdul Jabbar; Shampa Guha; Bithy Podder; Giorgia Gon; Sabina F. Rashid; Elissa Kennedy
articles.abstract: Menstrual health advocacy often states that harmful social norms influence adolescents' menstrual health. However, there is a lack of specificity in identifying which social norms drive menstrual behaviors and how these norms operate and are sustained. We carried out a phased qualitative study with adolescent girls in Khulna, Bangladesh, guided by Bicchieri’s (2017) social norms theory. The research team identified initial candidate behaviors, which were refined through three FGDs with mothers and five FGDs with girls. Subsequent data collection involved five FGDs with girls and three with boys, along with in-depth individual interviews (IDIs) with girls (n=15), mothers (n=7), fathers (n=3), and male (n=2) and female (n=3) teachers. Our framework analysis blended deductive coding against social norms constructs, including empirical and normative expectations, reference groups and sanctions, with inductive analysis to understand experiences. We found that a privacy norm influenced the concealment of menstruation and restricted discussions, limiting learning and support. A second influential factor was the expectation that a “good mother” teaches her daughter how to care for herself at menarche. Other behaviors, such as school attendance or care-seeking, were primarily influenced by non-normative drivers, including beliefs. Our results provide evidence and an applied theoretical framework to guide interventions. We emphasize that both empirical and normative expectations and sanctions must be identified and addressed in interventions aimed at shifting social norms. Our findings emphasize mothers and families as key reference groups and suggest interventions targeting girls alone may be unable to shift norms.

articles.title: The Social Life of R₀: Why the reproduction number is less a fact about a virus than a rumor about the society it lands in
articles.authors: Fabio Sanchez
articles.abstract: The basic reproduction number, R₀, is routinely reported as though it were an intrinsic property of a pathogen, a biological constant to be looked up and endured. It is not. R₀ is an average over a population, and its value is set largely by how that population lives: household size and age structure, density, housing and sanitation, work and mobility, and access to care. The same pathogen therefore carries different reproduction numbers across social settings, and the scalar R₀ obscures the contact structure that determines who is infected and where transmission will concentrate. None of this is news to epidemiologists; the confusion lives downstream, where a working average is repeated as though it were a fixed trait of the microbe. This essay argues that R₀ is best read not as a verdict a virus hands down but as a summary of the conditions a society arranges for it: in an outbreak, a map of where transmission will run hot; over the longer run, a lever held largely by sectors well beyond emergency response.

articles.title: Relying on the Mainstream? Entity Networks in Alternative Media
articles.authors: Paul Balluff; Hajo G. Boomgaarden; Annie Waldherr
articles.abstract: Alternative media, characterized by their heterogeneous nature and self-perceived corrective role to legacy media, have gained increasing relevance in shaping public opinion. Despite their influence, large-scale analyses of their referential and actor-related reporting characteristics remain scarce. This exploratory study investigates named entity networks in German alternative and legacy media, focusing on their reporting on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline from 2011 to 2022. Using computational methods, we analyze news articles from 37 alternative and 98 legacy outlets, extracting named entities and constructing co-occurrence networks to identify distinct reporting patterns. Our findings challenge assumptions that alternative media inherently diverge from legacy media in their referenced entities. While alternative media exhibit distinctive network structures—such as lower modularity and higher transitivity—they also demonstrate substantial overlap in their choice of entities and patterns of media mentions. These findings suggest that alternative media frequently mention other media, which may reflect resource limitations and reactive reporting tendencies. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of alternative media by highlighting both their unique characteristics and shared practices with legacy media.

articles.title: Arches of Discontent: The product vs feature problem of infrastructural residual space
articles.authors: Srijon Barua; Anonymous OSF
articles.abstract: In February 2019, Network Rail sold 5,261 railway arches to a Blackstone-led consortium for £1.46 billion, terminating the security of several thousand micro-enterprises, migrant traders, and arts producers. This article reads the transaction as a clarifying case of the asset-manager phase of rentier capitalism, in which publicly produced infrastructural value is converted into a securitized income stream through administrative decisions whose technical surface obscures their distributional content. Drawing on documentary analysis, site survey, and stakeholder interviews across London, Zurich, Kyoto, and Dhaka, the article identifies four institutional instruments through which infrastructural residual space is converted from feature of the urban commons to product extracted from it: discount rate methodology, rent-uplift trajectory, head-lease cascade, and statutory carve-out from security of tenure. Each of these instruments has a counterpart in regimes that produce different outcomes asking the question-what happens when infrastructure ends but the space remains? Commodity, or feature for community?

articles.title: The Social Stratification in Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Use Frequency, and Workplace Acceptance in 11 European countries
articles.authors: zhuofei lu; Yao Ma
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) has diffused rapidly across Europe, yet who feels able to
use it—and who is willing to work with it—remains poorly understood. Using the
latest CRONOS-3 panel of the probability-based European Social Survey (N =
7,556; 11 European countries, fielded in 2025), we model six separate measures
of GenAI literacy and use frequency, together with acceptance of GenAI as an
assistant and as a peer in the workplace, using country-clustered estimators with
wild-bootstrap inference. Acceptance is strongly role-differentiated: a majority
accept GenAI as an assistant, but only one in ten as a peer. Both competence and
acceptance are sharply stratified by education, age, and gender—and the gender
divide is the most consistent pattern of all: women trail men on every one of the
six literacy and use measures and on both acceptance outcomes, and the deficit
appears in behavioural use as well as in self-assessed skill, so it cannot be reduced
to gendered self-assessment alone. GenAI literacy and use frequency in turn
strongly predict acceptance in both roles. Cross-national variation is substantial,
but with only 11 countries no association between national media, scholarly, or
AI-talent environments and individual outcomes survives strict small-cluster and
multiple-testing corrections, so national context is treated descriptively. GenAI
competence and workplace acceptance thus emerge as socially stratified from the
outset—with women consistently furthest behind—an early-forming divide that
risks hardening as GenAI becomes workplace infrastructure.

articles.title: Authoritarian Environmentalism as Just Transition? A Critical Environmental Justice Examination of State Environmental Intervention in Northwestern China
articles.authors: KuoRayMao; Qian Zhang; Nefratiri Weeks
articles.abstract: Environmental justice for China’s rural populations is especially important in the context of China’s multifaceted environmental crises as existing disparities have exacerbated the unequal distribution of economic wealth and environmental harm between rural and urban communities. This chapter examines two environmental intervention programs in China to evaluate environmental justice outcomes under authoritarian environmentalism. Based on 136 in-depth interviews as well as government documents, official statistics, and reports from state-owned media in China between 2009 and 2016, our research demonstrates that the exertion of authoritarian state power in green transition may worsen environmental inequalities and dispossess the underprivileged rural populace in China. The findings indicate that just transition in China requires a multi-scalar examination on how state-led economic development initiatives and the material interests of the centralized bureaucracy shape the formulation and implementation of conservation programs and environmental regulation. We suggest that instead of viewing local communities as problems to be fixed by arbitrary administrative measures, the central state should utilize government organized NGOs affiliated with national ministries and grassroots environmental NGOs to incorporate community-based perspectives into program formulation and implementation. Institutional innovations that reconceptualize authoritarian state environmental intervention as constant responses and adjustments involving multiple stakeholders will be essential for just transitions in China and beyond.

articles.title: After the Stall: Botswana’s Resumed Fertility Decline
articles.authors: Duke Mwedzi
articles.abstract: After almost a decade of stagnation, fertility in Botswana resumed declining and is approaching replacement level. Though fertility stalls are assumed to be temporary, most of the literature has focused on explaining their causes. Less is known about how fertility changes after a stall, and register data in Botswana presents an unprecedented opportunity to study post-stall fertility with universal coverage. Using descriptive analyses and a finite mixture modelling approach, I examine the trends in childbirth between 2011 and 2023. Results show that the timing of childbirth is becoming more heterogeneous and stratified. Highly educated women are postponing first births while less educated women are accelerating them. Most children are born to unmarried mothers, and this share has increased. Fertility trends in Botswana are largely comparable to other late-transition contexts, and it may serve as an illustrative case for how other stalled countries will continue their transitions.

articles.title: Households’ regional housing affordability strain and mental health: insights from the Netherlands
articles.authors: Agata Anita Troost; Mark van Duijn
articles.abstract: Housing affordability pressures are increasingly recognised as a key determinant of mental well-being, yet existing research largely focuses on individual or household-level cost burdens, omitting the spatial context. This paper argues that housing market pressures are subject to regional market dynamics, shaping mental health in addition to individual housing affordability stress. We examine how regional housing affordability strain is associated with mental health in the Netherlands by combining LISS Panel survey data with geo-coded administrative data from Statistics Netherlands. We use a novel rank-based measure of regional price-income mismatch to capture the relative position of households within regional housing markets. Regression results show that regional housing market pressure is negatively associated with mental health in 2023, although no comparable association is found in 2018. The 2023 relationship persists after controlling for individual characteristics and household-level affordability stress. These findings suggest that the mental health consequences of the housing crisis extend beyond individual cost burdens, highlighting the importance of regional housing market dynamics as an independent source of stress.

articles.title: Beyond Interrogation: A Dialogic Autoethnography of Freedom, Security, and Competing Worldviews in Iran
articles.authors: Alibenabbas
articles.abstract:
Abstract

Social conflicts are often interpreted as disagreements over political or ideological positions. This article argues that many such conflicts emerge from deeper differences in the systems of meaning through which individuals interpret shared concepts. Using dialogic autoethnography, the study presents a composite analytical dialogue, developed from the author's lived experiences, long-term social observations, and multiple conversations within the sociopolitical context of contemporary Iran, to examine how concepts including freedom, security, justice, religion, and legitimacy acquire competing meanings within contrasting worldviews.

Rather than seeking to reconstruct a single historical conversation or privilege one political position over another, the dialogue serves as a qualitative interpretive device through which competing systems of meaning are explored. Throughout the narrative, factual, historical, legal, and social claims are supported, wherever possible, by academic scholarship and documented sources.

The dialogue progressively re-examines shared concepts through questioning and reflection, suggesting that meaningful dialogue becomes possible when the assumptions underlying apparently common concepts are made visible and reconsidered. The study proposes that durable social change depends not only on institutional transformation but also on critical reflection upon the worldviews and interpretive frameworks through which social reality is understood. Dialogic autoethnography is therefore presented as a qualitative methodological approach for exploring competing systems of meaning and facilitating reflective engagement across deeply divided perspectives.

articles.title: Gender-Based Homophily in Research:  A Large-Scale Study of Man-Woman Collaboration
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: We examined the male-female collaboration practices of all internationally visible Polish university professors (N = 25,463) based on their Scopus-indexed publications from 2009–2018 (158,743 journal articles). We merged a national registry of 99,935 scientists (with full administrative and biographical data) with the Scopus publication database, using probabilistic and deterministic record linkage. Our unique biographical, administrative, publication, and citation database (“The Polish Science Observatory”) included all professors with at least a doctoral degree employed in 85 research-involved universities. We determined what we term an “individual publication portfolio” for every professor, and we examined the respective impacts of biological age, academic position, academic discipline, average journal prestige, and type of institution on the same-sex collaboration ratio. The gender homophily principle (publishing predominantly with scientists of the same sex) was found to apply to male scientists—but not to females. The majority of male scientists collaborate solely with males; most female scientists, in contrast, do not collaborate with females at all. Across all age groups studied, all-female collaboration is marginal, while all-male collaboration is pervasive. Gender homophily in research-intensive institutions proved stronger for males than for females. Finally, we used a multi-dimensional fractional logit regression model to estimate the impact of gender and other individual-level and institutional-level independent variables on gender homophily in research collaboration.

articles.title: Students' Perceptions Regarding the Fairness as a Social Value (Author's English Translation)
articles.authors: Inna Gazieva
articles.abstract:
The aim of the article is to provide a sociological definition of fairness in the context of state policy to strengthen traditional Russian morals based on the results of using the author's empirical model of analyzing the students' perception regarding social values (Decree of the President of the Russian Federation No. 809 dated 11/09/2022). Methods. The theoretical and methodological basis of the research is an interdisciplinary synthesis of philosophical concepts of fairness and sociological theories of values, which made it possible to identify four dimensions of fairness value, such as ideal, desired, expected and real. Empirical testing was carried out on a representative sample of RANEPA students (N = 4338) as part of the online survey "Traditional and strategic students' values" (May-June 2023) by using a linear distribution analysis and correlation analysis (Spearman coefficient) of the sociological data. Results. The present study confirms integrity of fairness as a social value. The author revealed a high internal consistency of all its components (from the meritocratic ideal to real behavior). Furthermore, the systemic mutual relationship between fairness and responsibility, humanity, labor and cognitive activity is established. It became the basis for the operational definition of the concept under study, which now allows considering fairness not as an isolated attitude, but as the core of a value structure integrating personal and social orientations. Discussion. The author proposes a sociological definition of justice as a socially significant universal, manifested in a consistent system of attitudes and practices identified by an empirical model of social values analysis. The results are of direct practical relevance. It lies in providing an empirical model for monitoring the traditional value interiorization among young people and developing value education focused not on declarative assimilation of norms, but on the formation of an internally consistent value position that can become the basis for building a just society by means of personal responsibility and ethic interaction.

Author's English translation of the article published in Russian: Central Russian Journal of Social Sciences, 2026, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 81-99 (EDN RQSSEN). The Russian original is the version of record. Archived version of this translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21509404

articles.title: Value Basis of the Professional Potential of Students: Research Methodology (Author's English Translation)
articles.authors: Inna Gazieva
articles.abstract:
This article attempts to solve the problem of developing and applying a value-based approach to the formation of the professional potential of students, which is manifested in the contradiction between the need for a scientific approach to the formation of the professional potential of students, ensuring the stability of the state socio-professional reproduction system and its personnel sovereignty, and the lack of a scientific and methodological base sufficient for its study and subsequent formation. The purpose of this article is to describe the author's methodology for studying the value basis of the professional potential of students, as well as the results of its testing. The empirical basis of the study was the results of a sociological survey conducted by the author based on an empirical model of the analysis of the professional potential of students developed earlier (students of universities and branches in 36 regions of the Russian Federation; N = 3864); the data analysis was carried out using the descriptive statistics method. The article analyzes the attitude of students to the terminal and instrumental values of society declared by the state, which form the basis of the professional potential of students as their desired image, which, depending on the level of internalization, are distributed among structural levels. In addition, the article suggests a scheme for assessing the professional potential of students, which is a calculation of the integral indicator of the formation of two groups of values: terminal and instrumental. The article concludes that the value basis of the professional potential of students is very heterogeneous, which is explained by the specifics of the implementation of youth policy, while at the same time determining the prospects for its implementation. The proposed methodology can be used both during further study of the country's student youth and can be expanded to other socio-professional groups.

Author's English translation of the article published in Russian: Vestnik of Saint Petersburg University. Sociology, 2025, vol. 18, iss. 3, pp. 284-301 (EDN LPWJHD). The Russian original is the version of record. Archived version of this translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21508549

articles.title: The young and the old, the fast and the slow: a large-scale study of productivity classes and rank advancement
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: We examined a large sample of Polish science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and medicine (STEMM) scientists (N = 16,083) to study rank advancement and productivity in the past 40 years. We used two previously neglected time dimensions – promotion age and promotion speed – to construct individual lifetime biographical and publication profiles. We followed a classificatory approach and the new methodological approach of journal prestige–normalized productivity. All scientists were allocated to different productivity, promotion age, and promotion speed classes (top 20%, middle 60%, and bottom 20%). The patterns found were consistent across all disciplines: scientists in young promotion age classes (and fast promotion speed classes) in the past were currently the most productive. In contrast, scientists in old promotion age classes (and slow promotion speed classes) in the past were currently the least productive. In the three largest disciplines, the young-old promotion age productivity differential for associate professors was 100–200% (150–200% for full professors), and the fast-slow promotion speed productivity differential for associate professors was 80–150% (100–170% for full professors). Our results were partly supported by a regression analysis in which we examined odds ratio estimates of belonging to top productivity classes. To examine the sample, we combined biographical and demographic data collected from the national register of all Polish scientists and publication metadata on all Polish articles indexed in Scopus (N = 935,167).

articles.title: Beyond Gender Headcounts in Higher Education: A Multidimensional Justice Framework for Equality, Equity and Parity
articles.authors: Sixbert Sangwa
articles.abstract: Gender equality in higher education is commonly monitored through sex-disaggregated ratios, but numerical parity is neither a complete definition of equality nor a self-interpreting verdict on institutional justice. This critical integrative review examines how equality, equity, parity, formal opportunity, substantive opportunity, descriptive representation and substantive influence are conceptualised across higher education scholarship. A transparently bounded, PRISMA-adapted search completed on 23 July 2026 identified 58 records; after duplicate removal, screening and eligibility assessment, 26 studies and reviews were included. The synthesis reveals two recurrent analytical errors: headcount reductionism, which treats a 50:50 distribution as sufficient evidence of justice, and procedural formalism, which treats identical rules as sufficient evidence of fairness. To address both errors, the article develops a Multidimensional Gender Justice Assessment Framework integrating normative equality, access, resources, procedures, participation, outcomes, influence, intersectionality, temporal persistence and remedial justification. Application to a four-member committee demonstrates that the same numerical composition may be fair, unfair or indeterminate depending on how candidates entered the pipeline, how criteria were constructed and applied, and how authority is distributed after selection. Parity is therefore best treated as a sentinel indicator that prompts investigation rather than as a substitute for causal and normative inquiry. The framework offers higher education leaders a practical basis for auditing admissions, appointments, governance, academic careers and student participation while preserving both substantive equality and procedural fairness. It also specifies when targets, thresholds or temporary quotas are defensible: persistent disparity, an evidenced mechanism, proportionality, transparency, safeguards against tokenism and scheduled review are required.

articles.title: What large-scale publication and citation data tell us about international research collaboration in Europe: changing national patterns in global contexts
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek
articles.abstract: This study analyzes the unprecedented growth of international research collaboration (IRC) in Europe during the period 2009–2018 in terms of co-authorship and citation distribution of globally indexed publications. The results reveal the dynamics of this change, as growing IRC moves European science systems away from institutional collaboration, with stable and strong national collaboration. Domestic output has remained flat. The growth in publications in major European systems is almost entirely attributable to internationally co-authored papers. A comparison of trends within the four complementary collaboration modes clearly reveals that the growth of European science is driven solely by internationally co-authored papers. With the emergence of global network science, which diminishes the role of national policies in IRC and foregrounds the role of scientists, the individual scientist's willingness to collaborate internationally is central to advancing IRC in Europe. Scientists collaborate internationally when it enhances their academic prestige, scientific recognition, and access to research funding, as indicated by the credibility cycle, prestige maximization, and global science models. The study encompassed 5.5 million Scopus-indexed articles, including 2.2 million involving international collaboration.

articles.title: Defining Nature for Policy and Practice
articles.authors: Patricia Soranno; Stephen Posner; Courtney DeLoatch-Hill; Emerson Conrad-Rooney; Katie Arkema; Meena M. Balgopal; Gillian Bowser; Monika M. Derrien; Kevin C. Elliott; Tessa Francis
articles.abstract: What counts as "nature" is increasingly central to public policies, investment decisions, and scientific assessments, yet the term is often left undefined or implicit. Because nature is a complex, value-laden concept, a universal definition is unlikely to serve all uses, creating problems for comparability and auditability of claims. When users document what counts as nature and disclose the basis for their claims, measurement becomes more comparable, and accountability improves. We present a framework that pairs a concise definition with its purpose, context, and boundary rules, and apply it to develop a definition of nature that can reveal how benefits, harms, and stewardship responsibilities are distributed across people and places. Definitions should be treated as public commitments: articulating both a definition and a replicable process for revision makes governance more transparent, auditable, and open to legitimate contest.

articles.title: The Geography of Immigrants in Same-Sex Couples in the United States
articles.authors: Nathan Isaac Hoffmann; Kristopher Velasco
articles.abstract: The policy landscape for same-sex couples in the United States has changed rapidly in recent years, and the number of immigrants in same-sex couples have markedly increased. Little is known, however, about where these lesbian, gay, bisexual, and queer (LGBQ) immigrants settle and experience these shifting policy environments. Using American Community Survey data from 2008-2023 and original datasets, this paper studies the geographic context of immigrants in same-sex cohabiting couples in the U.S., comparing them to them to immigrants in different-sex couples and the U.S.-born in same-sex couples. We find that the distribution of immigrants in same-sex couples is expanding across the U.S. over time. Individually, these immigrants resemble U.S.-born LGBQ Americans, with higher incomes and educational attainment. At the geographic level, they appear more distinct, clustering in areas with more LGBTQ+ nonprofit organizations, greater numbers of immigrants, higher density, and higher property values than the areas that straight immigrants or the U.S.-born in same-sex couples tend to live in. Our findings contribute to a fuller understanding of this rapidly growing population and its unique characteristics.

articles.title: Intelligence as a Partial Order: Why g Compresses a Structure It Cannot Rank
articles.authors: Aaron Hoegn
articles.abstract:
The general intelligence factor "g" is one of the most, if not the most replicated constructs in
psychology, and its predictive validity is not in question. My question is its interpretation. The
positive manifold is the current popular proof that intelligence is a scalar, a quantity along which
people can in principle be ranked. I argue that such inference is wrong. Brains that have similar
functionality differ significantly in architecture, and the properties they differ on (efficiency,
specialization, cost, resilience) are particular trade-offs which form a Pareto front instead of a single
optimum. On this front each different architecture that "excels" in different environments is
incomparable to the others, as ranking them would require privileging a specific set of abilities to
reward, and for human life none is favored. Intelligence, thus, is better described as a partial order
rather than a line. Ranking remains legitimate between widely separated scores, where a whole-life
average lets a large gap dominate; within a band of equal g, it does not. This account returns a
prediction a scalar model cannot make: equally scoring individuals should cross over in
performance as demands change. It also names the core assumption whose failure would reinstate g
- that for a human life, no environment is privileged.

articles.title: A Youth-Led Co-Design Methodology for Digital Vaping Prevention
articles.authors: Kendra Nelson Ferguson; Bhargav Kandlakuti1; Gina Martin; Stephanie Coen; Tanya Iwas; Laila Girum; Saige Werstuik; Adrian Delgado; Adrianna Chong; Laura Struik
articles.abstract: Youth engagement is increasingly recognized as an important strategy for strengthening health promotion interventions, yet few studies provide detailed methodological accounts of how youth co-design can be implemented in practice. This paper describes the development and implementation of the E-Prevention And Vaping (EPAV) youth co-design methodology and examines how this participatory model functioned in practice. EPAV used a structured multi-stage co-design process that integrated youth co-researchers within the research team and engaged youth aged 15 to 24 in participatory workshops to develop vaping prevention messaging. An embedded convergent mixed methods process evaluation assessed participants’ experiences of the co-design process using post-workshop surveys that included closed and open-ended questions. Findings indicated high levels of satisfaction, perceived inclusion, and workshop effectiveness, as well as the importance of interactive activities, collaborative dialogue, and cultural grounding. These findings demonstrate how structured youth co-design approaches can support meaningful engagement while generating concrete intervention outputs for youth-focused health promotion initiatives.

articles.title: Off the Streets: Full-Time Schooling and  Property Crime in São Paulo
articles.authors: Augusto Alves; Bruno Pantaleão; Alei Santos
articles.abstract: The relationship between schooling and crime is well documented in the economics literature: more schooling means less crime. Yet the mechanisms behind this relationship remain an open question, especially in developing countries. We ask whether full-time schooling lowers crime by building human capital or simply by keeping students supervised, exploiting the staggered rollout of São Paulo's Full-Time Education Program (\emph{Programa de Ensino Integral}) across public schools between 2012 and 2024. Using \citet{callaway2021difference}'s doubly-robust difference-in-differences estimator applied to geocoded crime records, we find that adopting the full-time model reduces property crime in the surrounding area by about 7\% (18.8 fewer offenses per hexagon-year), an effect driven by robbery. The reductions are sharply concentrated in time and by offender: theft falls by 26\% during school hours but is, if anything, slightly higher outside them; effects are strongest on school days; and crimes committed by juveniles fall disproportionately --- roughly 65\% for theft and 23\% for robbery. Because the effects emerge precisely when, and for whom, school supervision is most binding, they are hard to reconcile with longer-run human-capital or opportunity-cost channels and instead point to incapacitation. Full-time schooling thus yields immediate public-safety gains in a middle-income setting, which is relevant to both education and crime-prevention policy.

articles.title: Inside of  Prosperity: How Japan transformed Growth to Development.
articles.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles.abstract: Exploring the strong influence of economic prosperity on the Japanese economy, the approach shows that the economy for example can naturally increase a strong and relevant capacity to influence the wealth generation in the economy in particular. The success of the Japanese economy shows the high combination of the strong coordination of the many strong policies, such as the economic policies, particularly supported by the strong influence of economic institutions. Japanese economy, particularly experienced a strong and influenced capacity to guarantee the high impact on the economy and the global economic context,on the other hand, the evidence shows that, without the most important and relevant basic conditions, the evidence shows that the Japanese economy for example, create the strong influence of institutions and strong capacity of growth GDP, using the coordination of policies. On the other hand, for example, the existence of the main basic conditions such as the natural resources and the human capital, are not naturally enough to enhance the development, this evidence is aligned with the existence of the main basic conditions in some economies such as the developing economy. Thus, have natural resources not means plausiblely the existence of the development capacity, this aspect are particularly helped from the behaviour that existed in the literature, particularly relatively with the existence of the many poverty countries with high natural resources and in the other hand with incapacities to create and generate naturally the relevant growth needed in particular. For example, some important examples are included of the Angola evidence, in line with the Democratic Republic of Congo.

articles.title: ‘The House of Health Literacy’ - a youth-centred model of health literacy developed through co-research with adolescents
articles.authors: Anna Wahl; Karolina Seidl; Sigrid Moick; Lisa Affengruber; Daniela Rojatz; Isolde Sommer; Lisa Stauch; Orkan Okan; Lisa Gugglberger; Ursula Griebler
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Health literacy (HL) is critical during adolescence, as this life stage is characterised by increasing autonomy in health-related decision-making alongside exposure to complex information environments. This study addresses the gap between adult-oriented conceptualisations of HL and youths’ lived experiences by co-developing a conceptual HL model grounded in young people’s perspectives.
Methods: A co-research approach was applied. Youth co-researchers were recruited using purposive, convenience, gatekeeper, and snowball sampling across diverse educational and community settings. 57 youth co-researchers aged 14–22 and four adult co-researchers participated in the co-research, reaching 182 adolescents. Peer interviews, focus groups, surveys, and co-research workshops were conducted by youth co-researchers independently and together with adult co-researchers. A photovoice sub-study addressed remaining data gaps. The data were analysed using grounded theory, combining initial coding by adult co-researchers with validation meetings and participatory analysis workshops involving youth co-researchers.
Results: A youth-centred conceptual model of HL—the ‘House of Health Literacy’—was developed, conceptualising HL as interconnected dimensions which, like the elements of a house, build upon and stabilise one another. Four dimensions are represented as floors of the house: (1) individual characteristics as the foundation; (2) spaces for information and communication on an online–offline continuum; (3) trust and relationships, which mediate how information is accessed and assessed; and (4) health information and health-related decision-making as the top layer, symbolising that the core HL process is built on the other dimensions. The fifth dimension, (5) society and trends, operates as an overarching influence, shaping all other dimensions.
Conclusions: The Youth-centred House of Health Literacy offers a novel perspective that challenges the adult-centred conceptualisations of adolescent HL. The model aligns with dimensions of existing frameworks while adding and highlighting youths’ priorities on HL.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Human Activity and the Natural Environment at the City Scale: A Case Study of Toyama City, Japan
articles.authors: Makoto Yamamoto; Futo Terashima
articles.abstract: Assessing the relationship between human activities and natural conditions at the city scale is useful for urban planning and sustainable development. However, in Toyama City, Japan, where densely inhabited districts (DIDs) and depopulated areas coexist, spatial analyses of this relationship remain limited. To address this knowledge gap, this study presents a spatiotemporal analysis of the relationship between rail transport and vegetation cover in Toyama City. Railway use and the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) were used as proxies for human activity and natural conditions, respectively. Changes in these proxies during 2011–2023 were visualized using a geographic information system. Results revealed an increase in both proxies in the central areas of DIDs, while areas outside DIDs exhibited heterogeneous patterns. Outside DIDs included locations where both proxies decreased, while others showed increased passenger numbers but decreased NDVI. These findings indicate that the relationship between human activities and the natural environment does not change uniformly across a city. Notably, the improvements in this relationship in Toyama City may be attributed to compact urban development in certain areas. Overall, this study presents valuable insights for policymakers to develop effective strategies for urban planning and sustainable development.

articles.title: Survivors in Science: A Comprehensive Analysis of Gender Disparities
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Łukasz Szymula
articles.abstract: We followed “survivors in science” – scientists who started publishing in 2000 and who continued publishing until 2020-2023 (N = 41,424). They authored 2 million articles (N = 2,089,097) with more than 70 million cited references (N = 73,118,395) and worked in 38 OECD countries. Our sample is a highly selective group of successful scientists: they have succeeded in persisting in science for more than two decades. Using a raw Scopus dataset, we examined gender disparities in publishing intensity, international collaboration, journal selection, productivity, citations, team formation, and publishing breaks in 16 STEMM and social science disciplines. Several author-level metrics were computed. Our data show only a single gender gap (related to publication productivity): lifetime scholarly output gap and annual productivity gap. The data do not show a gender international collaboration gap, a gender journal selection gap, a gender citation gap and a gender team formation gap for this specific sample of highly successful individuals. Men were on average 23% more productive than women cumulatively in 2000–2023 and 19% more productive in the last 5 years studied (2019–2023). Men and women published in equally prestigious journals, received the same number of citations (field-normalized), and worked in equally sized teams. In all, 80% of scientists in STEMM disciplines and 70% in the social sciences had published every year. Our data indicate interesting disciplinary differences in gender disparities.

articles.title: Top performers and top journals: Persistent concentration in scientific publishing
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Wojciech Roszka
articles.abstract: In this research, we analyze the relationship between publishing productivity and access to highly prestigious journals, treating publishing in top journals as a stratification mechanism selecting publishing elites. We study N = 144,314 Polish scientists publishing for 30 years (1992–2021) and their Nart = 433,546 unique research articles published in the period. Using bibliometric data from Scopus, we compare the scientists belonging to the top productivity decile (the upper 10%, termed top performers) and the remaining population of scientists (90%) by discipline and period (five six-year periods). We measure the share of publications in prestigious segments of journals, with particular reference to the 90th–99th percentiles, and we use nonlinear journal prestige-normalized productivity. Our results indicate that access to top journals (defined as the top 10% of journals indexed in Scopus) is powerfully and permanently concentrated in the group of top performers in all disciplines and periods studied. The differences between top performers and the other scientists are primarily of a qualitative nature: they are seen almost exclusively at the top of the journal hierarchy rather than in its bottom or middle segments. Our logistic regression models indicate the complementarity of quantity and quality: publishing intensity increases the probability of membership in the elite segment of top performers, especially when it is coupled with publishing in prestigious journals. Our results suggest that top journals function as selection gates to academic careers and that they function as durable mechanisms of elite reproduction in science.

articles.title: Women in Science: Measuring Participation in Europe Across Disciplines, Generations and Over Time
articles.authors: Marek Kwiek; Łukasz Szymula
articles.abstract: In this research, we quantify an inflow of women into science in the past three decades. Structured Big Data allow us to estimate the contribution of women scientists to the growth of science by disciplines (N = STEMM 14 disciplines) and over time (1990-2023). A monolithic segment of STEMM science emerges from this research as divided between the disciplines in which women’s share rose most rapidly – and the disciplines in which the role of women was marginal. There are four disciplines in which 50% of currently publishing scientists are women; and five disciplines in which more than 50% of currently young scientists are women. But there is also a cluster of four highly mathematized disciplines (MATH, COMP, PHYS, and ENG) in which the growth of science is only marginally driven by women. Digital traces left by scientists in their publications indexed in global datasets open two new dimensions in large-scale academic profession studies: time and gender. The growth of science in Europe was accompanied by growth in the number of women scientists, but with powerful cross-disciplinary and cross-generational differentiations. We examined the share of women scientists coming from ten different age cohorts for 32 European and four comparator countries (the USA, Canada, Australia, and Japan). Our study sample was N = 1,740,985 scientists (including 39.40% women scientists). Three critical methodological challenges of using structured Big Data of the bibliometric type were discussed: gender determination, academic age determination, and discipline determination.

articles.title: Legitimacy, Embedding, and Learning: A Framework for Scaling Up Complex Psychosocial Interventions
articles.authors: Jaakko Harkko
articles.abstract:
Objective: To propose a multi-level framework to facilitate the sustainment and scale-up of complex evidence-based psychosocial interventions across mental health, social care, and employment systems.
Methods: Integrative review of 41 empirical studies on contextual determinants of Individual Placement and Support (IPS) sustainment and scale-up, interpreted through implementation science, policy implementation research, and welfare policy literature.
Results: Three mechanisms were identified as crucial for sustaining and scaling up: Policy Legitimacy: normative acceptability and institutional compatibility that enables mandates and political-administrative authorization; Policy Embedding: coherence of multi-level, cross-sector governance arrangements that routinise the intervention beyond pilots; and Policy Learning: cumulative implementation evidence infrastructure enabling comparable measurement, feedback, and authorized adaptation.
Conclusion: The proposed Legitimacy–Embedding–Learning (LEL) Framework for Scale-Up holds that scaling complex interventions is a configuration challenge within complex systems, rather than a linear dissemination task. The framework may support proactive adaptation when scaling IPS and similar interventions.

articles.title: Towards a Theory of Performative Youth Representation: A Diagnostic Framework for Institutionalized Youth Governance
articles.authors: Jhayzen Tristan S. Morado
articles.abstract: Scholarship on democratic erosion documents institutional hollowing at the national level, but its operation in the sub-national micro-sites where citizens first meet the state remains comparatively undertheorized. Formally constituted youth governance bodies routinely produce performative rather than substantive outcomes, and existing frameworks built for presidents and legislatures were not designed to diagnose why. This paper asks why youth bodies holding real fiscal and legislative power still default to performative compliance, and how the same architecture generates the tactical resistance that contests it. It introduces Performative Youth Representation (PYR), a Five-Variable Dialectical Matrix in which legal, spatial, organizational, communicative, and evaluative constraints co-produce containment and subversion within the same institutional moment. Developed through the Philippine Sangguniang Kabataan — the most fiscally and legislatively empowered youth governance body in the comparative record, hence a hardest case under the Sinatra Inference — and engaging representation theory, participatory governance, and discursive and commons institutionalism, the framework’s signature persists across three statutory regimes despite rising empowerment, indicating a structural rather than resource-based mechanism. PYR states five falsifiable propositions and three scope conditions bounding its application, offering a transportable diagnostic tool for youth governance and advancing concept formation in governance research beyond the West.

articles.title: Anthony Giddens’s Sociology: Structuration, Modernity, Globalization, and the Politics of Reflexive Social Change
articles.authors: Mark Dorsett
articles.abstract: Anthony Giddens built one of the most ambitious sociological programs of the late twentieth century. This review reconstructs its chronology from suicide, class, and the classics through structuration theory, late modernity, self-identity, globalization, the Third Way, climate politics, and digital rights. It argues that the work is held together by a durable problem: how knowledgeable action recursively reproduces institutions across time and space while generating unintended consequences. The program matured by scaling reflexivity from situated conduct to institutional systems, biographies, global interdependence, and political steering. Its major achievements are the duality of structure, the temporal-spatial reconstruction of social order, and a relational account of trust, risk, and selfhood. Its limitations are ontological abstraction, weak causal discrimination, insufficient treatment of race, colonialism, gendered and classed inequality, and a policy turn that sometimes narrows earlier critical ambitions. The review identifies empirical afterlives and priorities for revising Giddens under digital and planetary conditions.

articles.title: Modelling Education for a Future We Cannot Assume: Four Structural Tensions at the Intersection of Artificial Intelligence, Cognitive Neuroscience, and Classroom Practice
articles.authors: Yanina Roman
articles.abstract:
The integration of generative artificial intelligence into classrooms forces a re-examination of assumptions that education has long left unquestioned. Access is no longer the central issue. What demands scrutiny is why identical tools yield divergent outcomes across learners — and what that divergence exposes about the cognitive and institutional architecture of schooling itself.
This paper develops an interpretive framework organised around four structural tensions rendered newly visible by AI's arrival, and proposes a reorientation of educational thinking from tool availability toward cognitive process, instructional sequence, and epistemic accountability. The first tension is a metacognitive gap: the benefits of AI access are mediated not by socioeconomic variables but by students' prior capacity for self-regulation, making equal access a systematic amplifier of existing inequality. The second is a friction paradox: the efficiency logic driving AI-assisted learning directly contradicts the desirable difficulty principles that cognitive neuroscience establishes as necessary for durable retention. The third concerns differential neuroplasticity — the as-yet unanswerable question of what sustained cognitive externalisation does to developing minds, a concern for which no adequate longitudinal evidence yet exists. The fourth is the epistemic collapse of assessment: the foundational inference from observable product to internalised competence has been destabilised in ways that detection tools cannot remedy.
These tensions are examined through a two-cycle practitioner inquiry (n=18) at a German-model international school in South America, during preparation for the Deutsches Sprachdiplom I (DSD I). A structured five-step AI-assisted practice sequence produced a mean gain of +0.8 points (Δ SK1→SK2), with marked internal dispersion. Students who improved by two or more points attributed their learning, without exception, to the teacher's initial explanation — the step preceding any AI involvement. Together, these findings suggest that instructional sequence matters more than tool availability. The challenge of preparing education for an uncertain future is not primarily technological. It is epistemological.

articles.title: Identifying Symbolic Modeling of Grooming Precursors in Social Media
articles.authors: Heath Landress
articles.abstract: Short-form video platforms such as TikTok and Instagram Reels increasingly circulate dating and lifestyle advice that may normalize coercive relational scripts, framing jealousy as devotion or secrecy as intimacy. A key challenge for preventing technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation is that early grooming precursors can be communicated through audiovisual choices, such as tone, pacing, setting, and editing, that make manipulative narratives appear benign. This qualitative multimedia content analysis identified recurring observable patterns of symbolic modeling through which relational and boundary-shaping cues associated with early-stage sexualized grooming are framed as ordinary dating or lifestyle advice in public TikTok and Instagram posts. Guided by Bandura’s social cognitive theory of mass communication, a purposive sample of 100 archival posts (50 per platform) was coded in MAXQDA using a structured multimodal observation protocol. Beyond its findings, the study contributes a transferable protocol for coding relational risk across visual, audio, and on-screen text channels simultaneously, extending grooming-detection methods beyond their text-only focus. Analysis produced a taxonomy of 10 recurring masking categories, derived from 289 operationally defined codes and interpreted through four themes. Masking operated primarily through presentation-layer conventions: simulated closeness, ordinary platform packaging, staged intimacy, and instructional framing dominated the corpus. Explicit grooming-literature cues were rare, appearing in 19 of 100 posts, and two cues, secrecy normalization and isolation, never appeared. Findings may inform prevention education and support future multimodal detection research.

articles.title: Beyond Compliance: Toward a Social Literacy Framework for Genuine Disability Inclusion in Japan and the United States
articles.authors: Islammd Shariful
articles.abstract: Current disability inclusion frameworks in Japan and the United States share a structural absence: the systematic education of non-disabled employees on how to interact with disabled colleagues with dignity and informed understanding. Both countries have developed legal compliance mechanisms (Layer 1) and organizational accommodation systems (Layer 2), while leaving unaddressed the social environment disabled employees enter after hiring. Drawing on 21 peer-reviewed studies and comparative legal analysis, this paper introduces the 3-Layer Inclusion Model as a novel theoretical framework for genuine workplace disability inclusion. The model proposes that inclusion requires a third, currently absent layer: the Social Literacy Layer — systematic, evidence-based education of non-disabled colleagues. Without it, legal employment produces the Dignity Gap: the distance between formal inclusion and lived inclusion — between employment and meaningful belonging. Empirical evidence from Japan confirms that stigma training significantly reduces colleague social distance (p < .05; Lem & Oyama, 2023), and that reasonable accommodation backfires when colleagues are not educated about its purpose (Handley et al., 2022). Cross-national comparison reveals that two countries with different legal architectures converge on the same Dignity Gap — indicating that legal framework design is less determinative of inclusion quality than the existence of Layer 3.

articles.title: Intergenerational Path Dependence in Media Literacy: A Structure-Practice-Cognition Multi-Mechanistic Framework
articles.authors: Wenjia Xia
articles.abstract: In highly platformized digital media environments, media literacy is widely regarded as a core competence for civic participation. However, substantial and persistent intergenerational differences can be observed in media interpretation, evaluative logic, and risk perception, which cannot be readily reduced through education or technological diffusion. Existing scholarship has largely framed these disparities as remediable “skill gaps,” yet such an approach fails to account for their long-term stability. Drawing on a path dependence perspective, this study develops a multi-mechanism analytical framework integrating structural conditions, social practices, and cognitive processes to reconceptualize the generational formation of media literacy. It argues that media literacy should not be understood as a neutral and cumulatively acquired individual competence, but rather as a socially embedded outcome shaped through the interaction of technological structures, everyday media practices, and cognitive lock-in mechanisms. Specifically, technological and institutional structures configure differentiated entry points into media environments; routine practices sediment these conditions into durable digital habitus; and cognitive mechanisms—such as preference stabilization and default effects—further reinforce existing pathways. The coupling of these mechanisms produces a self-reinforcing process of generational path dependence. By foregrounding this perspective, the study offers a theoretically integrated account of the persistence of media literacy disparities and provides new insights into digital inequality and generational fragmentation in the public sphere. It also carries implications for platform governance and media education policies aimed at enhancing intergenerational equity.
